**A.1. Executive Summary (Note: This 750 words; approximately 1.5 pages)**

Rwanda is ranked the first in Africa with respect to natural resource dependency and it is highly vulnerable to projected climate change impacts on natural resource dependent sectors. The agriculture sector accounts for about 32% of GDP, employs over 80% of the population and contributes more than half of Rwanda’s land area as agricultural and 95% of its rain-fed. The Eastern Province has the most agricultural land (41%) in the country, followed by Southern Province with 27%. The majority of the crops are grown under agricultural production depending almost exclusively on the amount of rainfall during the rainy seasons (mid-March to mid-December). In the past two decades, climate change has increased the frequency and intensity of droughts, floods and landslides affecting two million Rwandans. A combination of climate impacts, high levels of poverty and environmental degradation have made Rwanda one of the most vulnerable countries in Africa. The Eastern Province is among those with the highest vulnerability, most exposure to droughts and most severe potential reductions in crop production yields in Rwanda. The main crops grown are maize (80%), beans (15%) and cassava (5%). These crops are grown under agriculture and lack irrigation systems. From one severe drought in the period 1981 – 1993, the number increased to three from 2004-2016. The Eastern Province is also highly vulnerable to floods and landslides. When there are intense rains during the rainy season increases the risk of soil erosion and degradation, which increases the impact of drought in dry season. In Eastern Province the flood risk is linked to areas bordering the Akagera river.

The combination of increased temperatures for longer periods and decreased rainfall especially in the short rainy season, makes that the Eastern Province highly exposed to more dry spells with up to 7 days of dryness. There will be a decrease in crop water requirements and reduced soil moisture capacity. A study from ICGAR using the CGIAR CSM model estimated that by 2050 there would be a reduction of 16% in maize yields, 34% for beans and 87% for cassava by 2050 which will begin crossing critical thresholds in crop tolerance. Climate change, particularly dry spells and rainfall variability will exacerbate many of the ongoing degradation processes such as soil erosion, desertification, land abandonment, and reduced soil cover (primarily caused by rainfall) and further degradation. The Restoration Opportunities Assessment Methodology (ROADMAP) analysis in 2015 estimated that climate change could increase soil erosion rates by up to 30% globally, with the region responsible for approximately 21% of the soil erosion in the country. Since more than half of the Province is located on soils prone to wind and water erosion (soil loss potential > 50 tons/ha/year), it is estimated that climate change will introduce new degradation pathways through soil loss.

The impacts of climate change on agriculture and surrounding ecosystems is projected to result in serious socio-economic consequences. The agricultural sector, which accounts for approximately 21% of GDP and employs over 40% of the population could lose over 1% of its GDP each year due to climate related losses by 2030, and an even greater proportion (up to 5%) if no adaptation measures are taken. The projected economic costs associated with soil erosion loss and damage is to be in the range of USD 2 million and USD 7.5 million (RWF 1.9 billion and 8.6 billion) respectively per year.12 Smallholders will be the most affected group due to their lack of assets to buffer shocks and limited access to information, extension services and credit. The project proposes a range of adaptation actions in response to these climate change threats.

In response to these climate change threats, integrated adaptive measures are needed to enhance the resilience of the region’s ecosystems and landscapes and to support sustainable livelihoods for the rural population in the region in a manner that reduces poverty, increases resilience and achieves food security. The project's objective is to achieve a paradigm shift in land management practices in Rwanda's Eastern Province through the development and implementation of an integrated approach to address climate change to restored ecosystems and landscapes through building community resilience to enhance environmental services and livelihoods for the rural population. The project components and outcomes that will result in the achievement of this objective are:

Outcome 1: A shift to farming practices that build resilience against climate risks and threats.

Outcome 2: Strengthened adaptive capacity and reduced exposure to climate risks

Outcome 3: Strengthened institutional and regulatory systems for climate-resilient planning and development

In order to achieve these outcomes, the project will implement a range of innovative approaches13 that are adaptive and able to support transformation and innovative processes. The project Theory of Change (ToC) (Figure 3 shows how the project interventions will lead to the desired outcomes). The ToC is based on the assumption that technologies to build resilience of agro-ecological systems and livelihoods. Below the component structure and outcome implementation details.

Component 1: Restored landscapes that support climate resilient agro-ecological systems and livelihoods in Eastern Province, will scale-up tested and diversified landscape restoration and resilient agricultural practices such as agroforestry, intercropping, crop diversification, soil conservation measures (e.g. contour ploughing), plantations and ecologically critical buffer zones. Measures will restore ecosystem services and build resilience in drought-prone, degraded landscapes and thus achieve food security and reduce vulnerability of smallholder farmers

To climate change impacts and in particular soil erosion (during more intensive rainy seasons) and prolonged droughts. Restoration of degraded lands will increase overall productivity and reduce climate risks by improving the overall resilience of smallholder farmers to climate change, while also contributing to adaptation to future climate change scenarios and greater income security to ensure sustainability. These outcomes contribute together to overall drought resilience of smallholder farmers.

Component 2: Strengthened value chain management for climate resilient agricultural and tree products linked to financial products and services for sustainable management of agro-ecological systems, ensures the development of a robust enabling environment for the effective planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of climate change adaptation activities. This component will enhance the resilience and reinforces interventions under Component 1. Component 2 ensures that farmers and Farmer Forester Producer Organisations (FFPOs) are better positioned to add value to the agricultural products they produce through gender inclusive agricultural value chains and have access to appropriate financial services, including microfinance, credit and insurance. It will also support restoration activities as a means to improve adaptive capacity to climate shocks and loss of income induced by unpredictable weather patterns. This component will provide technical assistance for the development of cultural lending products to include short-term and long-term lending modalities combined with refined terms and conditions such as interest rates, collateral requirements, repayment schedules, etc., that are more appropriate for smallholder technologies, practices and value chains. This support will stimulate climate resilient investment (e.g., in forest technology) and the development of a robust enabling environment for the effective planning, implementation, monitoring systems and eventually link digitization to agri-lending tools. This will bring a paradigm shift in lending products and services that are more appropriate for smallholder technologies, practices and value chains.

Component 3: Strengthened enabling environment to effectively plan, manage and monitor climate adaptation activities. The objective of this component is to strengthen the institutional and policy enabling environment through developing systems, information and capacity for the effective planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of climate change adaptation activities. This will be achieved by ensuring that under component 3 will enable both better decision-making and better implementation as a result of stronger participation and accountability.

**II. Climate context (max. 1500 words, approximately 2 pages)**

Baseline scenario

Social, economic and ecosystems context

Rwanda is landlocked in East Africa and characterised by mountains in the west and savannah in the east, with numerous lakes and a temperate tropical highland climate. Rwanda's estimated population is about 13 million (2018). The majority of the population lives on less than $2 per day (2015) and more than 38% of Rwandans live below the poverty line with 16% living in extreme poverty. Female-headed households remain a challenge in the country. As many as 473,847 households (20% of total population) were considered food insecure in 2015.

In Rwanda, the agriculture sector accounted for more than 30% of GDP in 2014 and 80% of the population is engaged in the sector. While agriculture created less than 10% of new jobs in 2001 to 2011, it rose to 56% between 2011 and 2017 (World Bank). The country has a high dependency on rain-fed agriculture with limited irrigation infrastructure. The Eastern Province has the most agricultural land (439,000 ha) in Rwanda. Agriculture is predominantly practised by smallholder farmers who cultivate crops such as maize, beans, cassava, sweet potatoes and bananas.

Livestock

Rwanda has a livestock population of 12 million heads of cattle, with more than 85% being indigenous breeds. The country has about 31% of the total cattle population in 2015. Considerations include: the increased demand of milk with a limited land base; the need to improve feed resources and animal health services; the need for improved livestock management practices, grazing, and rashes to be progressively replaced by fenced ranches with dairy cross breed animals (0.5 ha/ha), providing higher return on investment than indigenous breeds; and the need to improve infrastructure in order to provide access to markets.

Livestock is currently the fastest growing sub-sector of the economy with an average growth of 8.3% per annum between 2010 and 2017 (World Bank). The livestock sector contributes about 54% of total agricultural output, which is dominated by smallholder farmers for about 31% of the total cattle population in 2015.

According to the EUCN Restoration Opportunities Assessment Methodology (ROAM) in 2015, approximately 37% (134,170 ha), or 21.2% of the soil erosion in the country. Land degradation is a result of a complex chain of direct and indirect drivers including: high population pressure due to rapid population growth; high pressure due to wood supply demand imbalance: demand of 1.65 M m³/year vs sustainable capacity of 0.55 M m³/year); over-exploitation of natural resources (e.g., water, land, timber, and wildlife); exposure to soil erosion/drought exposing fragile soil to land degradation; especially on sloppy areas; low carbon organic matter content in soils; high pressure due to livestock grazing; high pressure due to firewood collection; high pressure due to hot moisture and salt nutrients; over-exploitation of crop residues for energy or animal feed, without ensuring required return of nutrients; high pressure due to soil compaction; high pressure due to poor land management practices; high pressure due to microclimate. These drivers lead to loss of soil productivity (both for food and wood), loss of profitability and business opportunities, and loss of biodiversity.

The most vulnerable population is the one that lives in extreme poverty (37% of total population est., 12,665,115) in 2020. One-third of this population lives in poverty (37%) and 15% live in extreme poverty.

### Historical climate trends in the Eastern Province

#### Rwanda
- The historical climate of the country and between seasons.
- According to Rwanda's Third National Communication on Climate Change, following the climate trends were observed for the period 1961–2015 in the Eastern Province:
    - Mean annual rainfall has decreased by 250 mm per year. The region experienced severe rainfall deficits over several decades and a general trend of decreasing rainfall.
    - Seasonal change: Rainy seasons have become shorter and more intense, leading to a reduction in agricultural production due to increased flooding and waterlogging.

#### Burundi
- In recent years, higher temperatures, prolonged drought periods, and elevated rates of evapotranspiration have resulted in disturbances in the hydrological cycle and altered river flows.
- In particular, increased temperatures resulted in a high decline of Deficit Index (DI) values. The Eastern Province has experienced more frequent and severe dry spells than other parts of Rwanda.

### Project Target Areas

The target areas of the project experience the dual problems of rainfall deficiency and soil deterioration due to agricultural droughts. The increasing frequency of drought in the province reduces the amount of recovery time between dry periods or sometimes causes a complete loss of crops, leading to food insecurity. In 2015, 38% of the country's area was classified as highly susceptible to drought, while 42% of the country's area is classified with moderate to very high susceptibility.

Future climate projections Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of drought events in Rwanda's Eastern Province while contributing to increased rainfall variability, which local population depends for irrigation. Projected impacts will further compound an already-fringe situation in these areas unless major adaptation actions are integrated in the way landscapes are managed and used.
The Third National Communication on Climate Change used the new version of the stochastic weather-generating LARS-WG incorporating predictions from 15 GCMs used in the IPCC AR4 and was used to project precipitation data for 2050 (see Table 3.1). The results show:
- Mean annual temperature is likely to increase by up to 2°C/C by 2050, from the 1970 average. In addition, increases in mean monthly temperatures are projected across all months of the year.
- Mean annual rainfall will increase between the range of 0.1 and 1.24 mm, however during the short rainy season (March to May) there is a high probability that rainfall will decrease by up to 35% while during the long rainy season (June to September), it is likely to increase by up to 60%. This means that the number of hot days and night will likely increase with 17-31% (hot days) and 47-64% (hot nights), while dry spells in the short rainy season are likely to decrease.
The Eastern Province always receives a low amount of rainfall and such changes in rainfall and temperature alongside increased dry spells could pose potential water deficit in the province in the coming years. The increased occurrence of prolonged droughts will also have an impact on food security, especially for vulnerable groups living in Nyagatare District, Rwanda's Eastern Province, specifically Kayanza, Kirhe, and Nyagatare districts, leaving 44,000 households (some 225,000 people) food insecure.

While there is an expected decrease in rainfall during the short rainy season, runoff will be unevenly distributed. Projections show an increase in heavy-rainfall event frequency (7-10 percent) and intensity (0-11 percent by 2050). ## In a Sowing: G = Growing H = Harvesting

A study on impacts of climate change on the potential productivity of eleven staple crops in Rwanda has estimated that climate change under both RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 will have, on average, a negative impact on 11 staple crops, with the exception of three crops (maize, sorghum and cowpea). The results show that the potential yield of maize is likely to decrease by at least 20% under RCP4.5 and 30% under RCP8.5. Similarly, the potential yields of sorghum are likely to experience a reduction in yields of at least 10% under ICP 4.5 and an 15% under RCP 8.5. In addition, it is estimated that the potential yield of cowpea will decrease by about 20% under both RCPs. The magnitude of the impact from future climate change vary over space, with the most severe reductions in potential crop yields in the Eastern province.

The National Agricultural Research Institute (NARI) has developed a program called “Climate Smart Agriculture” which aims to boost productivity by improving inputs and extension services. Thus, this program may face additional challenges to achieve its objectives under future climate change conditions. The Ministry of Agriculture is currently developing a national strategy aimed at informing concerning where diversification of livelihoods and adaptation investments may need to be prioritized to support food security in the Eastern Province.

The analysis from the National Risk Atlas (2015) shows that the number of people vulnerable to severe drought are 28,562 and 157,786 for the agricultural seasons A & B respectively for the seven districts of the Eastern Province. Nevertheless, since the majority of these people live in the Southern Province which is a critical food basket of the country, the effect is likely to dominate the overall food security of the country.

The increase of total rainfall but also the intensity of precipitation during the rainy season are exposing lands on slope areas not yet protected by terraces and other soil conservation measures. This will lead to increased erosion in these areas(decreasing their resilience to drought in dry season), and increases the water and sediment runoff to the downstream areas.

#### Uganda Dairy Development Project: Effective Value Chain Development in Eastern Province

The Uganda Dairy Development Project (UDDP) is a World Bank funded project in the Eastern Province – in the Rayonge, Kagera, Gishu, and Kayanza districts where they have an established network of agriculture and enterprise development. The project will support the existing value chains by providing access to markets for dairy products.

The project focuses on five core areas: access to quality and reliable seeds, inputs and input finance; climate resilience and erosion control; improved livestock management practices; market linkages; and financial services. The project will also provide training in business planning and marketing skills.

### Forest Landscape Restoration in the Mayaga Region – UNDP and REMA

The project area is located within the Mayaga region (for 263,270 ha) with institutional and legislative frameworks guiding a forestation natural resource management and agriculture within the region alongside development of agroforestry. The project will cover approximately 15,000ha of forest. The intervention includes participatory forest management and private sector concessions for timber production. The project is expected to benefit over 23,000 people in the region.

The project has taken a number of lessons learned from the pilot landscape restoration plans as well as any institutional capacity for planning and implementing landscape restoration projects.

### Transboundary Agro-ecosystem Management Programme for the Kagera River Basin – FAO and MINAGRI

The project area is located within the Kagera River Basin in Rwanda, Tanzania, Burundi and Uganda. The project aims at enhancing and enriching agricultural productivity; minimizing risks to agricultural, livestock and forestry production systems; protection of natural resources and biodiversity; and increasing rural livelihoods through improved access to markets and other economic opportunities.

The intervention includes activities by farmer groups in adopting Agroforestry systems, trials on Soil fertility management, soil conservation and land husbandry, small-scale irrigation technology, line and compost, small stock management, genetic improvement, animal health services, and training. The project is expected to benefit over 105,000 people.

Specifically for Eastern Province,

### MIRAGA Irrigation Programme development:

The Government of Rwanda has embarked on a substantive water management programme in the Kagera River Basin pipeline in Eastern Province. This program consists in supporting several water management and water supply schemes such as the Musanze Multi-Purpose Dam (USD 173,558,019), the Wangata Irrigation Scheme (USD 263,856,832), the Gatore-Mugungu Irrigation Scheme (USD 40,000,000), the Musanze Multi-Purpose Dam (USD 73,255,000), the Kagera River Basin Pipeline (USD 19,233,550.00), the export targeted modern irrigation project (USD 120,500,000), the Gatore-Irrigation Scheme development project (USD 48,760,000).

### Regular Programmes and earmarked funds for agricultural development Eastern Province by MINAGRI and IMU:

A number of regular programmes are being implemented in Eastern Province. These include soil conservation and land husbandry; small-scale irrigation technology, line and compost, small stock management, genetic improvement, animal health services, and training. More specifically, output 1.1 of TREP project builds on the existing Twagiru Muhanzi Farmer Field School system which has been customized (improvement of the organization of farmers groups, awareness and establishment of Mulzi, preliminary agroforestry tree planting practices).

# Rawa Dairy Development Project (RDDP): Funded by IFAD ($US 65.3 Million)

## Background

The RDDP was started in mid-2018 with a view to strengthening the dairy value chains in 12 districts, including 4 districts of Eastern Province (Nyagatare, Kabale, Kayonza and Rwanjana). The project aims at increasing milk production by at least 50% among smallholder farmers. This is to be achieved through promotion of improved the production technologies, increased access to markets, and enhanced value chain development.

### Objectives

The RDDP has three main objectives:
1. Increase dairy productivity by at least 50%, mainly from smallholder farmers.
2. Increase income by at least 80% among participating smallholder farmers from dairy farming, through improved production technologies, increased access to markets and enhanced value chain development.
3. Strengthen the institutional framework for dairy value chains in Eastern Province.

### Project Components

The RDDP project builds on the experience of the FAO funded TREPA project (2015-2018) which was implemented by the same implementing partners, organizations: facilitating linkages to markets and dairy value chain actors. The RDDP project builds on the experience of the FAO funded TREPA project (2015-2018), which was implemented by the same implementing partners.

### Adaptation Scenarios

The project will be adapted in response to climate change, as it does not sufficiently factor into climate change impacts of the landscape and ecosystem level in the Eastern Province. This leads to increased vulnerability of farmers to drought (high risk for all farms) and flooding (moderate risk for all farms).

### Project Components

1. Smallholder livelihoods are resilient and more adaptive to climate change, in particular in the context of increased droughts.
2. Market access is improved through better linkages with markets and value chains.
3. Ensuring finance is available to support the development of climate resilience across value chains.

### Project Activities

The project will be implemented by:
- Strengthening dairy production systems on arable lands, while restoring and protecting more fragile lands and addressing the dual climate induced problems of rainfall variability and soil erosion.
- Promoting agroforestry practices in degraded lands to improve land productivity and resilience through landscape-scale restoration of degraded lands improved by climate risk assessment, management and finance. The project will be implemented on a landscape scale with each targeted piece of land.

### Land Use

For each targeted piece of land, the best restoration option according to its location and roles (potential impact in the water catchment area, floodplain, or downstream areas) is identified. This will include agroforestry practices (priority) and stronger rains during the rainy seasons. The agroforestry and forestry activities will target degraded lands on sloped areas with high erosion risk and low soil fertility. These areas are characterized by poor land use management and the better coverage of soil by good forestry agronomic practices will reduce significantly the risk of soil erosion during intensive rain events.

### Land Use

The project will also focus on improving livestock grazing areas in the downstream plains, naturally already exposed to some flooding in intensive rain seasons. For these plain areas, the project will promote agroforestry and silvopastoral activities (priority) and improved land use management practices such as contour ploughing in upland areas in rainy season, in downland areas in dry season). The traditional open free grazing of livestock on degraded lands has led to overgrazing of these areas. This will be addressed by the introduction of improved grazing systems (e.g., one-head per 10 ha) and a reduction in stocking density from 5-7 heads/ha to 2-3 heads/ha.

### Land Use

On public lands under special protection status (middle side, Akeza buffer zone), participatory approaches engaging neighboring local communities will be employed to restore the most degraded lands. The targeted degraded buffer zone is a priority area for climate change adaptation and mitigation as it has high soil erosion risk and low resilience and reduced run-off.

# Key climate hazards for the Eastern Province: projected impacts, landscape restoration interventions and adaptation results.

## Climate change projections and impacts for the Eastern Province

### Increasing trend in mean temperatures
- Leads to increasing significant water stress.
- Increasing heat stress affects livestock productivity.
- Increasing heat stress increases disease pressure on crops.
- Increasing disease pressure on crops leads to a reduction of optimal thermal optimum for pathogens, which together with a number of indirect effects will reduce crop yields.

### Decreasing trend in mean rainfall and number of rainy days coupled with more intense rain events
- Late harvest, delay of sowing in the dry season, and low yield.
- Reduced grazing and feed resources during long dry spells significantly affect food security of cattle farmers by reducing their ability to access forage from livestock pastures, leading to soil, thus challenging the sustainability of livestock production systems.
- Droughts destroy existing soil conservation structures such as terraces on hillsides and lakes and ponds thus afflicting fish populations.

### As rainfall variability is related to climate change, it will reduce water storage and availability, affecting both human and livestock water supplies during long dry spells, while groundwater recharge diminishes.

## Project adaptation interventions

### Promotion of agroforestry practices:
- Promotes the integration of trees into croplands and their recharging through the creation of sheltered microclimates.
- Increases soil organic matter that contributes to soil fertility.

### Promotion of silvopastoral practices:
- Promotes the integration of trees into livestock systems, which update the landscape with a greater diversity of species.
- Reduces nutrient runoff from fertilizer and increased nitrogen leaching in pastures.
- Silvopastoral systems enhance the resilience of pastoral systems to nutrient loss, and climate change, while increasing soil organic matter content through the regulation of the hydrological cycle.

### Restoration and sustainable management of degraded lands (including Alakura bauxite zone) by promoting agroforestry practices such as establishing anti-erosion ditches on slopes, planting trees for wind erosion, meiothermic material, the water table is increased, limiting flood risk.

This framework implies a question and a line of investigation that GCF partners and the GCF will pursue through the projects risk management process. ### Adaptive management

Adaptive management frameworks are specifically designed to adapt to projected climate change impacts. There is an element of future climate impacts within and beyond the GCF project life, which may require the adjustment of interventions as well as updating or modifying the project design. The framework will help to identify opportunities for adaptation during implementation by engaging key players intervening in the Eastern Province, which may contribute to an increase in project size and scale. As such, adaptive management is a critical component of the Rwanda project. It will be implemented through five pathways: 1) identifying and implementing actions that will enhance the ability of decision-makers to plan for climate change; 2) monitoring and evaluating actions will increase the ability of decision-makers to form timely responses to new information; 3) learning from experience will improve the quality of future decisions; 4) adaptive management will provide a basis for long-term sequencing of proposed measures before committing resources to adaptation decisions during implementation.

### B. Theory of change (max. 1000 words, approximately 2 pages plus 2 appendices)

#### Barrier analysis: Rwanda has advanced in many aspects of mainstreaming and implementing climate resilient initiatives. However, there are still significant barriers that need to be addressed in order to achieve less effort or less effective actions, missed opportunities and/or higher costs for future adaptation strategies (table 3). These barriers include:

- **Knowledge barriers**: Limited baseline data on site and vulnerability of ecosystems and vulnerability of human livelihoods due to climate risks. Knowledge barriers refer to the awareness and understanding by farmers, value chain actors and others of how climate change will impact their livelihoods and what they can do in response to these impacts. The rural population is largely unaware of the risks that climate change poses to their livelihoods, such as reduced crop yields, increased pest pressure, and changes in rainfall patterns. This lack of awareness leads to a sense of vulnerability of human livelihoods or difficulty to calculate and track information for making evidence-based investment decisions and adaptation strategies. Farmers are also not aware of how to adapt their livelihood practices to climate change impacts becoming insufficient in the context of climate change. Farmers have limited awareness of climate resilient production methods as well as the ability to implement them, which is a barrier to mainstreaming climate resilience into agricultural production. This lack of knowledge leads to decision-making processes based on climate forecasts. Such information is usually available from the Rwanda Meteorology Department (RMD) and other sources such as the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). However, there are limited practical guidance on how to adopt alternative and innovative practices to adapt livelihoods, agriculture and land management in response to climate change impacts. This lack of knowledge leads to decision-making processes based on climate forecasts.

- **Impact pathway analysis**: Impacts of climate change can be direct or indirect. Direct impacts include changes in temperature, rainfall patterns, and extreme weather events such as floods and droughts. Indirect impacts are those that result from the direct effects of climate change, such as increased soil erosion and land degradation. These indirect impacts can have significant consequences for agriculture, water resources, and human health.

- **Technical / capacity barriers**: Technical assistance services have limited technical skills, information, knowledge to design and implement adaptation solutions related to landscape restoration & soil and water management in the face of climate change - including the ability to identify and implement more resilient practices. People living in Eastern Province lack the skills to implement agroforestry, silvopastoral systems, and other land use practices that can help to reduce soil erosion and land degradation.

#### Technical / capacity barriers

- **Limited technical capacity**: The technical staff and communities in the Eastern Province of Rwanda have limited technical capacity and knowledge on how to design and implement adaptation solutions related to landscape restoration & soil and water management in the face of climate change. This lack of capacity leads to decision-making processes based on climate forecasts.

### (3) Farmer organizations are weak and have insufficient capacities to design integrated climate resilient solutions to address climate change impacts on access markets and value chains that would livelihoods and protect against climate shocks

- **Farmer vulnerability**: Farmers, especially women and young people, are organized and often underrepresented in the market and do not enjoy benefits to support healthy livelihoods.
- **Lack of farmers associations and groups**: This impedes their participation in equitable markets and access to finance. Lack of financial services (e.g., loans, grants), access to equitable markets and engagement with value chains, lack of knowledge on climate impacts, vulnerabilities and adaptive capacity enhancement through resilient agricultural practices, and limited access to information and extension services.
- **Impact**: These factors can compound the effects of climate change and exacerbate environmental degradation such as soil instability and nutrient loss.

### Social, cultural and gender barriers

- **Dependence on monoculture and subsistence agriculture in PD**: Slows down the rate of adoption of diversified agricultural systems as adaptation options. Dependence primarily on seasonal crops, such as maize, sorghum beans, and cassava, is a major barrier to diversification.
- **Women's role**: Women are more vulnerable than men because they occupy much space on the fields and compete with crops for nutrients.

### Traditional gender roles and patriarchal attitudes towards women in rural Rwanda mean that women have limited control over resources. This makes them more vulnerable to shocks and stresses linked to climate change. Women’s involvement in certain livelihoods is also limited by cultural norms, which limits access of women to land or certain farm households.

### Financial barriers

- **Limited knowledge on climate change and experience financing resilient agricultural practices**: Farmers lack the necessary skills and knowledge about climate change and practices are still too high for farmers to operate and manage water supply and invest in agricultural inputs and tools.
- **Cumulative deterioration resulting from climate change**: The cumulative deterioration of soil fertility, coupled with increasing rainfall variability and in particular femerations no longer have the capacity to adapt adequately in innovative climate resilient land and soil management practices. This makes it difficult for farmers to access credit or other financial services that are critical to be able to bear the incremental costs of addressing the severity of climate shocks on small-scale infrastructure.
- **Uptake of climate-resilient technologies**: The Government of Rwanda has made significant progress in promoting the uptake of climate-resilient agricultural practices and technologies. However, there is still a need for financial services providers to support farmers with access to finance and investment resources for climate change adaptation.

### Any Introduction

The project will provide tailored technical support and capacity building to communities in the Eastern Province to develop appropriate and gender-sensitive climate-resilient restoration activities. Capacity building will include training on selection of adaptive measures, training on selection of appropriate adaptation measures will take place through public meetings and workshops. The project will also provide information on the state and vulnerability of ecosystems and biotopes, potential for ecosystem degradation and loss of biodiversity. Training and tools and investments will be made in climate resilient land use practices such as agroforestry, buffer zones and clean and efficient cooking technologies through a pilot project. The project will also provide technical support to communities to implement the agroforestry system to universalize agroforestry and simultaneous cropping techniques and help them to understand the benefits of agroforestry in terms of climate resilience. The project will provide information on climate resilient species seed and seedling supply to support output (5.1.4). The project will also provide technical support for the development of a gender-sensitive adaptation plan that includes climate-resilient solutions (enhanced knowledge and information system). Once the pilot project is completed, the project will scale up the successful interventions across Eastern Province.

### B.2 Projecting/Project description (max 3000 words, approximately 4 pages)

#### Objectives
The project objective is to shift land management practices in Rwanda's Eastern Province from landscapes that are degraded, fragile and unable to sustain livelihoods in the face of climate change to restored ecosystems and landscapes through building community resilience to enhance livelihoods, food and water security of the most vulnerable rural population.

The project will be implemented in the Eastern Province, which is most vulnerable and drought exposed region of Rwanda.

#### Project Components
The components of the project are as follows (Figure 4):

- **Component 1:** Strengthening landscape restoration to create resilient agro-ecological systems and livelihoods in Eastern Province.
- **Component 2:** Market and value chain development for climate-resilient agricultural and tree products linked to financial products and value chains.
- **Component 3:** Strengthening institutional capacity to effectively plan, manage and monitor climate adaptation outcomes from improved land use at national and decentralized levels.

The project will pursue an integrated resilience approach that is adaptive and able to support transformation and innovative processes. Component 1 will scale up tested restoration practices to build resilience in drought-prone, degraded landscapes and landslides-prone areas of the Eastern Province. Component 2 ensures the economic and financial sustainability of the implemented practices for climate resilience and reinforces market linkages between producers and consumers. Component 3 aims at strengthening institutional capacity to effectively plan, manage and monitor the upscaling of the restoration model.

A gender transformative approach has been mainstreamed across the project design. The project design is guided by the principles of gender equality and women's empowerment in line with Rwanda's National Gender Policy and ensuring that the project provides women and men with an equal opportunity to build resilience, address inequalities and achieve sustainable development outcomes.

The three project components are described below (for detailed activity level breakdowns please refer to E.O.). The Feasibility Study (Annex 2) and other annexes provide additional detail and elaboration for the activities and sub-activities that are presented in summary form in the below description of the project components.

Overall, component B evaluates the interlinkages between investments, knowledge and experience developed during the implementation of the various restoration land uses and interventions and improved land use planning delivered under output 3.1 for the District Forest Management Plans and simplified Distinct Forest Management Plans and output 3.1.3 detailed Silvopastoral Plans, agroforestry plans and other land use plans (Output 3.2). These linkages create an enabling environment for improved land use planning and investments in the District.

The District land uses, plan, the district development plans, and national land-use plans will serve as a key reference during implementation for developing the forest restoration and silvopastoral plans. The process will be two-fold. First, in consultation with stakeholders, the District Forest Management Plans (DFMP) will be developed. Second, the DFMPs will be used to identify where the proposed land uses – in the existing plans - will be set of priority/second. The resulting maps will be validated and finalized by the District Government and approved by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Section E.6 provides detail about the activities listed below as well as the associated sub-activities and deliverables.

Output 1.1 Diversified Agroforestry packages are scaled-up (See RFA JUC). This intervention will address the lack of knowledge and capacities to implement climate resilient agroforestry landscape restoration interventions in the District. During project inception, potential interest groups/communities will be identified. These stakeholders will be selected through existing thematic maps and then prioritised based on community participatory mapping, pilot testing and other relevant information. The DFMPs will identify areas where these communities can implement their own tree nursery and demonstration plot (1-2 ha). 160 farmer groups will agree to sustain agroforestry systems in the District. This will be achieved by providing training and technical assistance on agroforestry practices, access to inputs, access to innovative financial services contracted/residence investments and under Component 2 Government staff will provide support to communities to establish demonstration plots and to provide ongoing technical assistance for the management of resident varieties. Support will be provided practices that reduce farmers' vulnerability to crop losses caused by adverse weather conditions. The intervention will also promote the adoption of more diversified, climate resilient livelihood options. Promoting agroforestry practices such as biomass incorporation into soil, intercropping and mixed cropping systems, use of drought tolerant species, and other best agricultural practices including drought-resistant species that can grow to maturity with less water use, while supporting soil nitrate retention and nutrient cycling will be promoted. The intervention will also address the selected tree species, planting methods and end-use pitches selected specifically to encourage soil and water conservation, improve soil fertility and enhance biodiversity. The DFMPs will identify areas where these groups will be supported to diversify nursery stock and some to establish demonstration plots through technical backstopping, involving training on seedling production, nursery management, tree planting techniques, post-planting care, pest and disease management, data collection and documenting lessons learnt will be integrated into activities under component 3. Particularly, the DFMPs will identify areas where these groups can implement their own tree nurseries and demonstration plots (1-2 ha) barriers to adopt and scale up investment in agroforestry packages, the project builds on the existing Twente Muhimu Agroforestry Project (TMAP) which has been implemented under Component 3 of the RFA DFMP database. #### Output 1.2: Woodlots and tree plantations are rehabilitated and sustainably managed for productive and ecological services (EES)

This intervention will result in highly productive, climate-resilient woodlots and forestland with fully restored ecosystem services and functions. The objective is to achieve the following: a) reduced soil erosion and sedimentation losses; b) increased evapotranspiration (with related water regulation impact) and decreased soil productivity, the objective of the proposed intervention is to achieve this through i) rehabilitation of degraded smallholder woodlots within district 10 and 20, ii) adoption of efficient, integrated and sustainable management systems and iii) enhanced marketing linkages for wood products, and access to credit facilities under Component 2. The project will also aim at promoting the use of agroforestry practices to reduce problems of land degradation from soil erosion and reduced moisture content and fire through tree and shrub establishment in degraded areas and on farms with low tree cover in the Eastern Province landscapes. The increased woodlot productivity will support narrowing the supply and demand gap in wood biomass in the Eastern Province.

The proposed intervention aims to restore 1,400 ha of very degraded district forests, to improve sustainable management of approximately 10,000 ha (5% of the Eastern Province total) of State forest land through long-term concessions to private investors under Component 2. The project will also aim at restoring and sustainably managing 37,648 ha of private smallholder woodlots managed by RFA PIs under Component 2. A total of 10,590 ha (28%) of the private smallholder woodlots to be managed under TAFI agreement with RFA PIs by contract holders will be financed through financial services under Component 2. For the case of State Forests, a concession agreement will be signed between the private forest company and the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism (MNRT) for the duration of the project period on a per-forest basis. Grant investments will be made available for FFPDs to manage more costly restoration actions (including anti-erosion measures, soil moisture conservation, fire prevention and control, etc.). The project will also aim at supporting district governments of Kayanza and Nyagatare and private owners to develop Simplified Forestry Management Units (SFMUs) under Component 2. SFMUs are a legal entity that allows for the management of forest resources by local communities in partnership with the MNRT. They will also support district governments of Kayanza and Nyagatare and private owners to develop Simplified Forestry Management Units (SFMUs) under Component 2. SFMUs are a legal entity that allows for the management of forest resources by local communities in partnership with the MNRT.

The restoration project will be implemented through the use of exotic species (Eucalyptus and Pinus), but the restoration will be done with more diversified high value timber species (including Natives) adapted to drought and avoiding over-exploitation. The main objective is to improve forest productivity, increase water retention capacity and reduce soil erosion; woodlots are essentially constituted by Eucalyptus, which is the preferred species of farmers due its coppicing capacity. The use of native species will be encouraged in order to diversify the timber production and to avoid over-exploitation of the current area. To mitigate any risk on water use, the project will ensure the selection of species/strains which are adapted to the local conditions and climate. In addition, the project will aim at reducing soil erosion by removing tree stumps and small branches to secure the increase of soil organic matter; avoid big clear cutting during dry season, etc.

A particular attention will be given for the proper involvement of women and men in these forest restoration and management activities through gender sensitive approaches, as described in the annexed Gender Action Plan (see page 102).

**Output 1.5 Clean and efficient cooking energy technology promoted through support to private sector and communities**

One of the main drivers of land degradation in the Eastern Province is extremely high pressure on wood resources for cooking, heating, and other domestic uses. This has led to overexploitation of forest resources and a major constraint for private forest growers to respect management plan prescriptions and avoid over exploitation of degraded areas. The proposed activities will support the development of clean and efficient cooking technologies that would be quick, which can be possibly only through ICS dissemination as recommended by the Rwandan Biomass Energy Strategy (RBES). This will reduce pressure on wood resources for cooking, heating, and other domestic uses.

Output 1.5 will deliver a large-scale awareness campaign across the Eastern Province on selected improved cook stoves (ICS) and their benefits. The campaign will be supported by the private sector and communities through the following:

- **Wood gasifier stove** (such as the "TURU Karunuma" model)
- **Improved fixed-mass stove**

Output 1.5 complements the supply side activities of Outputs 1.1—4 by reducing the supply-demand gap facing Eastern Province ICS users. In particular, the ICS communities will reduce the pressure on wood resources (bushes and agroforestry trees). This will allow woody owners to respect the harvesting rotation period established by sustainable forest management plans. The activities are supported by the interventions in Outputs 1.2—3 ICS business development and promoting the adoption of improved biomass cookstoves for rural farmers in the projects areas and through the promotion of agroforestry resources use and prevent overexploitation of wood resources.

# Co-Financing: USD 141,323 confirmed

The tasks of climate change adaptation and mitigation from land use activities mainly depends on farmers and local communities to identify risks and vulnerabilities as well as to adopt and implement appropriate economic and behavioral change incentives. Evidence in EP shows that behavioral responses to hazards heavily depend on the availability of resources and information. If farmers do not perceive economic benefits or if they are not convinced by economic incentives, they will be less likely to take active actions to reduce their risks or to adopt adaptation measures.

### Outputs in Focus

Outputs 2 and 3 focus on strengthening FPPOs at collective level and individually based on the perception of climate risk, paired with adaptive community organization, capacity building, and access to information. The outputs are also aimed at enhancing the enabling conditions in and around targeted landscapes for the implementation of adaptation actions, while using knowledge, information management and scaling of best practices developed by other project activities (Output 1). These outputs will be implemented through a combination of financial mechanisms and services that will be incentivised through economic benefits through engagement in production of timber, fodder and honey for example.

### Strengthening FPPOs

Strengthening FPPOs at collective level and individually based on the perception of climate risk (Outputs 2.1) and strengthening FPPOs to act collectively and to benefit economically from both diversified production systems and enhanced ecosystem services (Output 2.3). Financial mechanisms will be provided through a combination of grants, loans, and subsidies for members and independent farmers, based on promised ICT services promoted and information systems strengthened nationally and regionally in the ECP region. These financial mechanisms will support collective action at landscape level to strengthen chain activities in the Eastern Province, while financial mechanisms and support services will all agricultural value chains (Output 2.3).

### Component 2: Financial mechanisms and management capacities of FPPOs

- **Component 2.1:** Strengthening FPPOs at collective level and individually based on the perception of climate risk and that was about account overall resilience and overall sustainability of restored landscapes (Output 2.3).
- **Section E, Output 2.1: Financial mechanisms and services as below, as well as the associated sub-activities and deliverables** Further elaboration can be found in Annex 2A flexibility study.

### Output 2.1 Farmers' groups strengthened to adapt climate resilient land use practices with access to market and finances (ECE/ECN)

This output will strengthen existing or support the establishment of new FPPOs (district-level cooperative, farmers associations, forest user groups, producer organizations, farmer field school groups, savings groups, and other smallholder organizations) to implement climate-resilient land use practices. The project will also provide technical assistance for the development of an enhancement programme for resilient livelihoods and environment benefits. FPPOs will be strengthened to actively represent their members in decision-making processes at all levels (national, regional, district, and local). This will help them to better manage climate risks with the aim to protect and improve their outputs in the long-term. Through financial literacy and management training, FPPOs will also be able to access and use credit facilities for investment in climate-resilient land use practices and other agricultural products (Output 2.3). Additionally, the FPPOs will allow better servicing of their members and independent farmers through improved access to market information and services, as well as financial services. This will help them to improve farmers' reliance on government and donor support and facilitate access to national climate data platforms and restoration finance. The project will also provide training for FPPOs in the use of mobile money and other financial inclusion services. Financial service providers participating in the program already have financial inclusion strategies for women, and these will be integrated into the project.

### Output 2.1.1 Incentives targeted farmers into existing FFPs or where appropriate from new ones

Activities in component 2 are expected to mobilize USD 10M of lending by local financial intermediaries. This leveraged co-financing is not included in the budget for this component, and cannot be confirmed prior to project implementation. It therefore has not been presented in the budget totals.

**Output 2 Enhanced financial inclusion and investments in climate resilient value chains (IEU / IICA)**

The output addresses barriers such as limited financial products to stimulate climate resilient production in agriculture for FLR, and lack of access to finance for smallholder farmers and SMEs. It will also address the need for increased and overreaching limited financial participation in climate resilient production methods in respective value chains of the private sector. Interventions will be designed with a focus on increasing financial inclusion and investments in climate resilience through: (1) developing financial products to increase access to finance for smallholder farmers and SMEs; (2) building local capacity and knowledge for climate resilience in value chains; (3) developing financial products and improving access to loans for progressive farmers including FLR, agroforestry, and tree crops; (4) increasing the number of financial service providers and linking them with service providers and linking private sector service providers with farmers and FFPOs and down-stream value chain actors engaged in climate resilient production methods. The output will also address barriers to scaling up climate resilience through: (1) developing financial products for FLR, agroforestry, and tree crops; (2) building local capacity and knowledge for climate resilience prospects for a gradual shift away from grant finance to private operations.

## Component 3: Strengthened enabling environment to effectively plan, manage and monitor climate adaptation outcomes from improved land use at national and decentralized levels.

### Co-Financing: USD 13,538,421

#### Output 2.1 Strengthened gender-sensitive climate resilience for landscape restoration plans (EEF/ACON)

This output aims to design and implement gender-informed landscape restoration plans (Component 1) and livelihoods supporting Component 2 restoration plans in all seven districts in the Eastern Province Districts of Tanzania.

The project will adopt a strategy for mainstreaming based on the following three pillars:

* **Mainstreaming into policy:** This will be achieved by informing the development of national climate change adaptation strategies, sectoral policies, and guidelines.
* **Mainstreaming into planning processes:** This will involve integrating landscape restoration plans in all seven districts in the Eastern Province Districts of Tanzania. related to data to support climate-informed decision making. Therefore, the intervention aims to firstly approve knowledge and information systems needs based on findings of the feasibility study and initial activities under Output 3.1 and then develop new monitoring and reporting systems for different sectors and at all levels. The intervention will also aim to develop a new project tracking data system that will track the MRV for activities under Outputs 1.1, 2.1 and other outputs, as specified in this proposal.

The proposed measures ensure the integration of climate-related data to contribute to climate-informed decision-making, monitoring and reporting for different sectors and at all levels. Training will be provided to staff from districts agencies, RAB, RFA, RFAP, IOM, FARM, IFAD, FAO, WFP, MEF, and other relevant stakeholders on the use of climate information systems. By establishing such user-friendly climate information systems for the Eastern Province such as Forest Landscape Restoration (FLR) project will be able to monitor the progress towards achieving its objectives. The intervention will also support the FLR project will monitor the progression of relevant climate-related indicators at landscape level (Output 3.1). This will guide decision-making and planning activities within the Eastern Province and the rest of Rwanda. Specific activities under this Output include the following:

* **Sub-national knowledge exchange platforms and workshops to ensure effective integration of climate risk related data to support climate-informed decision making:** The intervention will provide training for staff in district agencies, from RAB, RFAP, IOM, FAO, WFP, MEF and other relevant stakeholders on managing information systems and integrating climate-related inputs.
* **Output 3.2 Seed and seedling supply systems are enhanced to provide diverse climate adapted species and varieties (IE: RFAP, IOM):** The intervention will address the limited knowledge and access of climate-resilient planting materials adequate to future climate scenarios used in agriculture, forestry and horticulture. It will further focus on improving the currently inadequate consideration of climate change impacts in seed selection and supply systems. This will be achieved by: (i) developing a climate resilient seed selection framework; (ii) establishing climate information networks and an information portal for habitat suitability for up to 100 climate resilient tree species and one crop species in Rwanda; (iii) organizing training workshops and training. This intervention will also improve the capacity of local entities to supply germplasm for native and resilient plant species, including trees, shrubs, grasses, and crops. The project will engage with key stakeholders such as the National Board of Forestry, Forest Research Institute, Rwanda Forest Authority, Ministry of Agriculture, paragovs suited to the agroecological zones in the Eastern Province. In parallel, the project will encourage the development of a climate-resilient seed selection framework and an information portal for habitat suitability for up to 100 climate resilient tree species and one crop species in Rwanda. The project will also engage with key stakeholders such as the National Board of Forestry, Forest Research Institute, Rwanda Forest Authority, Ministry of Agriculture, paragovs suited to the agroecological zones in the Eastern Province.
* **Output 3.4 Evidence from best practices generated and disseminated (IE: RFA, IOM, ENABLE):** The intervention will provide training for staff in district agencies with agricultural extension services with agricultural extension services to generate knowledge relevant to addressing specific farmer needs to adapt to climate change. The intervention will also aim to improve inter-agency knowledge about the role of agriculture in climate change mitigation and adaptation. This subcomponent will address knowledge gaps on agroforestry systems (e.g. ecological and socio-economic perspective, value chain development, etc.). It will also provide evidence from best practices generated and disseminated by RFA, IOM, ENABLE, and other partners. The intervention will aim to: (i) develop a climate-resilient tree species and crop varieties; (ii) test user-friendly improved cooking stoves (CCs) and produce 4 knowledge products on the use of CCs in Rwanda; (iii) conduct capacity building sessions for 8 and develop 6 knowledge sharing tools. The results from this applied research will both public and private development partners to disseminate appropriate agroforestry-based practices for land restoration; (iv) conduct capacity building sessions for 8 and develop 6 knowledge sharing tools. B.4. Implementation arrangements (max. 1500 words, approximately 3 pages plus diagrams)

The local Ministry for the project will be the Ministry of Environment (MoE) through Rwanda Forests Authority (RFA). Previously the Rwanda Water and Forestry Authority, has now been split into the RFA and Rwanda Water Resources Board (RWRB). The MoE functions and its related activities will be undertaken jointly by programs hosted at Headquarters (HQ) & GFO Coordination Unit. These HQ functions and related activities will be implemented through three Executive Units (EU), namely RFA, ENABLSI and IUCN-Rwanda office. In the HQ GFO Coordination Unit, these EU functions and related activities will be coordinated by a Project Coordinator (PC) who is responsible for: a) ensuring that all EU and HQ GFO functions are aligned with project objectives; b) preparing work plans and budgets, agreements with co-financers and each executing agency/priorities and procedures; c) providing technical support to the PC for project funds received; d) ensuring that the project complies with the terms agreed in the project respective FQA as well as the MoE guidelines, at least one before the mid-term National Steering Committee (NSC) meeting and one prior to the end of the year NSC meeting. IUCN HQ & ENABLSI are all will be EEU (RFA, Enablsi, & IUCN-Rwanda). A project Executive Unit receives project specific resources from HQ GFO and is responsible for: a) ensuring the supervision of the HQ as the AE; Service providers (ICPM, WFP, and ICCO) also contracted through HQ GFO; b) providing technical support to the PC for project funds received; c) ensuring that the project complies with the terms agreed in the project respective FQA as well as the MoE guidelines, at least one before the mid-term National Steering Committee (NSC) meeting and one prior to the end of the year NSC meeting. HQ GFO & ENABLSI based on successful delivery and acceptance by the EE signing the respective contracts (see Table 5). IUCN HQ & ENABLSI will be responsible for all project related activities in Rwanda, including the management of staff assigned to HQ GFO upon successful delivery and acceptance by the EE signing the respective contracts. Co-financers who are not directly part of the EEU or Service provider will choose to either sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on behalf of the EE or Service provider as a co-finance.

As IUCN Rwanda has a write-in in the project execution, a firewall will be established to ensure responsibilities are segregated so that no one person is responsible for both the financial and technical aspects of the project. This firewall will be implemented at HQ’s office based in Kigali only when HQ has taken on execution responsibilities. These include the responsibilities related to the project implementation, including but not limited to: a) ensuring that all EU and HQ GFO functions are aligned with project objectives; b) overseeing the project execution function including decisions made by the steering committee will be performed by the IUCN regional office for Eastern and Southern Africa which is in charge of coordinating the oversight function, including conducting supervision missions and providing technical support to the PC. The IUCN HQ GFO will provide technical support to the PC with staff outsourced from the regional office for Eastern and Southern Africa and Headquarters. The technical part of the project implementation will be performed by HQ GFO with staff outsourced from the regional office for Eastern and Southern Africa. All staff related to performing oversight will have their responsibilities clearly defined in terms of their roles and responsibilities based on the financial and non-financial functions during the performance of their duties under this project.

EEs will be in charge of the actual delivery of the project under the guidance of the AE and steering committee, more specifically:

EEs will be in charge of overseeing the tasks within the overall project management structure consisting a) Implementing day-to-day procurement activities directly or through the Programme Management Unit (PMU); c) Managing contracts of suppliers and services providers; d) Ensuring that all procurements are carried out in accordance with the GCF procedures, including the preparation of project work plan; and f) Carrying out financial and technical monitoring of activities, including the achievement of the outputs and results.

EEs will work with service providers at the activity level. Service providers will be either identified during the appraisal process of the project or selected through a procurement process. When identified during the appraisal process, the service providers will have their contracts signed by the AE.

The Secretary, Muli, will chair the National Steering Committee (NSC), which will provide implementation guidance and support as required to ensure that the project is delivered in accordance with the approved project document. The NSC will consist of three members (namely the three EEs with the support of the three service providers ICCO, WV and ISAFI), with consolidated financial and technical reporting on the project being submitted by the NSC to the AE for approval.

All funds disbursements will be made in accordance with requests from the PMU, governed by the GCF procedural requirements. All funds disbursements will be made through the PMU, which will ensure that all procurements are carried out in accordance with the GCF procedures and financial reporting has been accepted by the team in charge of oversight. The project task manager will coordinate feedbacks from the NSC on the progress of the project, including the submission of interim financial and technical reporting, and on the budget and work plan for the forthcoming disbursement request, the latter will be accepted, through official communication from the task manager to the PMU.

The strategic guidance and financial reviews and recommendations for the project implementation will be provided by the NSC comprised of key entities appointed by the Director General, RFA. All funds disbursed under the GCF will be subject to final approval by the National Contact Point (NCP) in charge of the output or activity. The National Steering Committee will meet twice a year.

Along with the three EEs (FRA, ENABEL and SUCI), the GCF will include the SPI (Single Project Implementation Unit) to the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning, selected representatives from among: the Ministry of Agriculture (MINAGRI); National Agricultural Export Development Board (SODEXNA); the Agaléga national park; representatives of CSOs107 and relevant private sector organizations. In addition, any other relevant representative may be invited to participate in the SPI.

Project Management Unit: The Project Management Unit (PMU), established under the RFA will perform according to the policy framework and guidelines issued by the NCP. The PMU will be led by a Director selected through an open competitive process by a panel appointed by the NSC on a Terms of Reference approved by the NSC. The establishment, staffing and operation of all PMU staff will be done following IUCN standard practices and proposed to Ministry of Environment for non-objection.

The PMU may include experts from local and international agencies identified based on project needs with the concurrence of the NCP. The PMU will also include representatives from other agencies operating in Seychelles such as CENAF, and other specialized entities will be linked to PMU through this modality.

The Programme Director is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the PMU within the guidelines last laid down by the CENAF. The Programme Director will ensure that all project activities are carried out according to the approved work plan and decision-making on possible actions if required and update the status of these risks by maintaining the project risk log.

The Project Implementation Unit (PIU) is responsible for implementing the project in accordance with the guidelines subsequently approved by the NSC. The AIPW indicates which activities should be funded by the RFA applying the Government procedures and regulations, including those related to procurement, finance, human resources, and social as part of the project.

The PMU will be established in Kigali at rfa MuM with its management structure and responsibilities outlined in the chart above. The PMU will provide the NSC with quarterly progress reports and close its operations when the final project terminal evaluation report and financial closure are completed.

The PMU will further include the leads for three Project Components. In addition, the PMU will be staffed with required professional and technically qualified personnel selected and recruited following IUCN procedures and presented to the Ministry for non-objection.

For ground level delivery, under the PIU, the executing entities together with support from these service providers will establish a Joint Action Development Forum (JADF) in each of the five Provinces of Rwanda. These teams will work closely with the Joint Action Development Forums (JADF) based in each district.

The PMU will develop the contracts, guidelines and technical documentation to engage and support the LDT, and implementing partners and members of local communities. NSC will provide policy direction and guidance to improve the coherence and efficiency of project implementation.

Each ILDT must be managed by an Area Manager reporting to the PMU via the three outcome leads, who convene appropriate implementing partners for the work in the area as directed and supported by the relevant Project Component teams. The LDTS will work closely with the Joint Action Development Forums (JADF) based in each district.

Coordination: The project, at the local level will coordinate closely with district and divisional coordinating committees to ensure that the project is aligned with national priorities and strategies. District Environment Directors (DEDs) are expected to play an active role in project implementation, facilitation and monitoring which is generally an assigned function of this office and play a key role in the grievance redress mechanisms, as described in the Environmental and Social Management Plan of the project.

#### B.5 Justification for GCF funding request (max. 1000 words, approximately two pages)

**Why is Project Proposing GCF Funding?**

The Government of Rwanda is aware of the risks of climate change as exemplified by Rwanda's national environment and climate change policy of 2019. The Government of Rwanda already has policies, strategies and plans in place to mitigate and adapt to climate change. However, the country still faces significant challenges related to climate change. For example, the country has invested in heavy irrigation schemes in areas that are prone to flooding due to increased rainfall intensity. However, these schemes are threatened by erosion from surrounding hillsides due to increasing extreme rain events.

The Rwandan Government does not have the financial means to implement all activities identified to improve climate resilience and requires additional technical support. The project cannot be accomplished without GCF support. Funds from GCF for TPIA/REAC

While project partners are contributing co-finance for the implementation of this project, this represents only a fraction of the total cost. The project will also require additional funding to implement adaptation capacity building training and practices to ensure that landscapes that support climate resilient agro-forestry systems are restored and maintained. This will be achieved through the involvement of smallholder farmers and communities who have resources and capacity to restore, benefit from, and maintain climate-resilient landscapes.

### Rationale and level of concessionality

The project is designed to address market failures in pricing and demand for commodities (section B.1). The vast majority of land is privately owned and densely populated. Limited community institutions, poor market structure and poor infrastructure translate into poor agricultural productivity and low income levels. This results in a situation where smallholder farmers are unable to access markets because the cost of grants for roads, lorries—since little surplus produce are produced and traded on cross-border or export markets—and it is inadequate to secure or service any loans. In this regard, prevailing market conditions necessitate GCF support to ensure that the project can be implemented in a manner that will enable smallholder farmers to access markets. The production/retention models are bought by financial viability to be maintained by private sector. For another important output, the project seeks to increase the level of concessionality for all grant supported measures is demonstrated in the economic returns from forestry and landscape restoration activities provided in Annex 3.

The Economic and Financial Analysis spreadsheet - Annex 3 shows the conclusions of the economic analysis, together with related assumptions and information. Best practices in appraisal for public sector projects have been followed.

### The net present value (NPV) of the project-level investment is calculated using a discount rate of 12.1%. This figure represents the minimum return that would be required by investors to justify their investment. The level of concessionality for this project is justified as this is the ratio at which the Government would have to borrow to fund equivalent investments in the absence of GCF support. The project has been performed using alternative discount rates of 8% and 20%, (the latter being higher than the average commercial borrowing cost).

Project costs include GCF investment co-and co-finance from partners and Government during the period projected as presented in Annex 4 (Detailed Budget Description). It also includes continued Government financial support for the remainder of the 20-year project.

Project benefits include the cumulative net financial benefits for participating farmers compared to business-as-usual, as well as the environmental benefits such as increased tree cover and other non-financial benefits like the value of time savings and environmental protection.

The project return varies depending on the period of analysis. The figures below present the NPV and Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) for a 20-year investment horizon. For an estimated 20-year Investment Horizon, Given the project's focus on long-term agroforestry landscape restoration and conservation activities, the 20-year investment lifetime is considered most appropriate for this analysis.

## Key non-market benefits from the project include the following:

- Reduced topsoil erosion**
- More water release for household needs, drinking and irrigation (Wilson and Lovell, 2016; Gentry et al., 2010); this is equivalent to a reduction in flood risk mitigation (e.g. Mathews et al., 2004; Rimmer et al., 2004).
- Time savings, especially for women and girls traditionally collect fuelwood;
- Household income increases due to reduced time spent collecting fuelwood.
- Reduced GHG emissions from the use of non-renewable biomass as a cooking fuel.

Non-market benefits are valued using shadow prices that attempt to reflect the amount that people would have to pay to obtain an equivalent benefit with the market. The main non-market-benefits quantified in this analysis are the GHG benefits from reduced deforestation and emissions avoided from the use of non-renewable biomass as a cooking fuel.

The design and prototype testing of such instruments are currently underway in collaboration with local governments, private sector actors, development banks and financial institutions. Alongside this, private companies and investors that are willing to operate in the area and provide relevant finance.

**Small local capital market:** Restoring a local capital market is necessary work, with laws of direct investment, access to credit, and other regulations. The project will also seek to strengthen the capital accounts. Attracting investment to the country and building up capital is crucial. A priority for the project is to ensure that farmers can obtain credit from financial institutions and that they do not necessarily all need to provide relevant finance.

**Need for strengthening implementation capacity:** The financial and human capacity to implement the initiatives planned is currently weak, with a lack of skills and knowledge regarding environmental management and economics. There are generally low levels of skills and knowledge regarding environmental management and economics.

Taking these points into account the concessionality that the GCF provides is justified.
