## How the project programme sustainability will be ensured in the long run

The project's exit and sustainability strategy are formulated on the integration of the landscape restoration and management activities with other development priorities, such as food security, agroforestry, and value chains for restored agricultural and tree products. The project establishes the enabling conditions necessary for long-term reduction in climate vulnerability and adaptation to climate change through a combination of landscape restoration and management (e.g., agro-forestry). Empowering national and local stakeholders and institutions to maintain these measures beyond the conclusion of the project is critical. This will be achieved by strengthening their capacity, including their ability to access finance for generating access to markets and finances, enhancing financial inclusion and access to responsible finance and private sector investment in landscape restoration and management activities. The project also aims at creating a conducive environment for climate resilient and adaptive economic development in the Eastern Province, which will in turn further enhance revenue generation and attract investments beyond the scope of the project. For full details of the project exit strategy refer to section 6.

The project ensures that the sustainability of the interventions is feasible beyond the GCF resources through the following transformative actions:

### Environmental sustainability

- **Restoration and livelihood and food security outcomes:** Restores the biophysical conditions of the drought-endangered Eastern Province into climate-resilient ecosystems and communities through a shift towards agroforestry, sustainable land management practices, and improved water use. This will lead to an increase in resilience of ecosystems to climate change by supporting water and soil protection while contributing to plant and soil carbon sequestration.
- **Energy and energy production materials:** Through Outputs 1.1-1.5, establishing long-term legal structures and capacity (under Component 2) for the project's landscape restoration activities, including land tenure arrangements with farmers (farms), local authorities, sector extensions and researchers under Component 1 (see section 6 and B of the Feasibility Study). The project will also make a contribution to the development of the Eastern Province’s energy sector by restoring forests and land ecosystems that are critical for water supply and agriculture development. Through its component 1 and the restoration activities supported by the GCF, the project will make at projects related to agriculture development and/or water management and supply such as those funded by the World Bank Global Food Security Programme and the Malnutrition (malnutrition).

### Policy, regulatory and institutional capacity

The transformative change established by this project is the development of the institutional capacity of stakeholders and institutions, particularly RFA as a lead executing entity to implement the green growth strategy and policy. The project will support the development of a national forest landscape restoration monitoring system that will develop and implement climate-risk-informed landscape management strategies. Increased knowledge on biophysical resilience for coordinated cross-sectoral landscape restoration planning and implementation will be supported by the project through 1) supporting a gender-responsive climate resilience for coordinated cross-sectoral landscape restoration plans under Output 3.1, and 2) developing a national forest landscape restoration monitoring system that will develop and implement climate-risk-informed landscape management strategies.

### Monitoring, evaluation and learning

Component 2: A focus on knowledge generation, dissemination and application through monitoring, and evaluation across the project activities informs the implementation of current and future adaptation efforts. The project will support the development of a national forest landscape restoration monitoring system that will develop and implement climate-risk-informed landscape management strategies.

### Sectoral monitoring and reporting mechanisms

These activities are instrumental to ensure that lessons learned, and best practices are shared among stakeholders in the sector. These activities are aligned with the outputs under component 1. Overall, these activities will lead to a systematic consideration of climate change risks and adaptation in policy development and implementation across all sectors.

### Forest Landscape Restoration Monitoring System

In particular, the project’s Forest Landscape Restoration monitoring system is aligned with and built on two existing monitoring systems: the District Forest monitoring information system (DFMIS) which has already been developed and now operational; and the National Forest Monitoring Information System which is connected with the District one. Both UGK and ENABEL have committed to integrating this new monitoring system into their respective national forest monitoring systems, in line with international commitments as well including NDCs forest and agroforestry related targets.

Capacity development measures will be provided through training sessions at central, district and local levels for key stakeholders such as performance contracts and monthly round tables to facilitate the collaboration for adaptation actions between institutions.

Training includes sessions at central and district level, to enhance capacities for funding mobilization, planning, and delivery of climate-resilient projects. Training will also include capacity building for project design, implementation, and restoration planners and managers. Trainings will be provided for managing information systems and integrating carbon accounting into the project cycle. The training will be conducted by a team of experts from GCF.

Training combined with technical assistance will also be provided to develop the capacity of district authorities in 7 target districts to identify priority areas for climate-resilient projects, including restoration activities. Technical assistance includes capacity building for the design and implementation of a cross-sectoral monitoring and reporting system that allows communities to define priority criteria and select primary target intervention areas to restore ecological functionality.

The project supports a variety of ICS technology interventions. Under Component 1, the project will work towards achieving the following objectives: (1) to support the development of an enabling environment for policy makers and policy shapers; (2) need to use existing technologies in order to achieve the following: (1) reduce GHG emissions from high carbon intensity sectors by promoting a shift to clean & efficient ICS and fuels. Each proposed ICS technology will be selected based on its ability to meet the project’s objectives, including cost-effectiveness and environmental benefits; 3. technology development will be supported through training local artisans and small-scale business entrepreneurs as well as providing technical assistance for the design and implementation of a cross-sectoral monitoring and reporting system.

The project will also establish "Cooking fuel and technology" hubs in 14 main local markets of TREPA intervention area.

Under Component 3, the project will establish a large-scale experiment in participatory development that emphasizes market-based approaches to scaling up ICS technologies. The project will support the design, testing, and deployment of priority technologies, implement the field tests and assume responsibility for disseminating the results locally.

The total budget funding for capacity building is approximately 4.0 million USD and technology development transfer is 5.6 million USD.

D. EXPECTED PERFORMANCE AGAINST INVESTMENT CRITERIA

This section looks at the performance of the project/programme against the investment criteria as set out in the GCF’s Initial Investment Framework.

### D.1 PROJECT OUTCOMES (approximately 3 pages)

The proposed GCF project contributes to increased climate-resilient sustainable development. More specifically, the project seeks to reduce the exposure of Rwanda’s Eastern Province to the impacts of extreme weather events (including severe flooding and droughts) by increasing the resilience of smallholder farmers and woodlot growers in the region against these hazards.

#### Project Outcomes

The project provides GCF-sensitive measures to address the adaptation needs of small farmers’ and woodlot growers’ livelihoods. The project will increase food security, improve access to basic infrastructure (the project will benefit directly 506,232 people (4.4% of the national population) and an additional 18.2% of the national population), and provide a range of ecosystem services (e.g., water regulation and flood control). It is estimated that the project will reduce food insecurity by increasing access to basic infrastructure and improving livelihoods, which in turn will contribute to increased resilience against extreme weather events.

The project provides GCF-sensitive measures to address the adaptation needs of small farmers’ and woodlot growers living in the Eastern Province. The project will benefit directly 506,232 people (4.4% of the national population) and an additional 18.2% of the national population). The beneficiaries of the project will be smallholder farmers and woodlot growers living in the Eastern Province. The project will also provide GCF-sensitive measures to address the adaptation needs of women and girls as part of the project beneficiaries considering their important role in rural agriculture.

The project has been designed to deliver on the adaptation goals set out in Rwanda’s NDC and to contribute to three of the GCF’s adaptation results areas:

- **GCF adaptation results area 1 (A1) - Increased resilience of vulnerable people, communities and regions.** The project will develop actions in strategic agroecosystems that are not only support the restoration of ecosystems but also provide a range of ecosystem services to smallholder farmers and woodlot growers living in the Eastern Province of prioritized communities. In support of these actions, FFPOs, considering gender mainstreaming, will be organized and strengthened with the aim of increasing their capacity for climate change adaptation and resilience building and ensure that government extension service providers have the knowledge and tools to deal with the effects of climate change on agroecosystems in the Eastern Province. The project will also provide GCF-sensitive measures to address the need to develop forestry, agricultural, agroforestry and conservation activities through which ecosystems and livelihoods resilience can be increased against extreme weather events.

- **GCF adaptation results area 2 (A2) - Health and well-being, and food and water security.** The project will improve food and water security by supporting climate resilient agricultural and livestock practices that are less susceptible to extreme weather events. These practices include the use of drought-resistant crops, improved irrigation systems, and conservation of water resources through rainwater harvesting. The project will also provide GCF-sensitive measures to contribute to increased food security by increasing access to basic infrastructure (e.g., roads) which in turn will contribute to improving food security by decreasing runoff and enhancing rainfall during rainy periods, and conserving water resources.

- **GCF adaptation results area 4 (A4) - Increased resilience of ecosystems and ecosystem services.** The project will provide GCF-sensitive measures that support the restoration of agroecosystems in the Eastern Province through land conservation and the regulation of hydrological cycle by promoting landscape restoration activities (agriculture, forestry, agroforestry, etc.). These actions are expected to increase resilience against extreme weather events such as droughts. Such restoration actions from the project will reduce erosion, decrease loss of soil organic matter, and thus increase water retention in the Eastern Province.

Table 8 shows how the expected adaptation impacts from the TREP4 project contribute to the achievement of the GCF Core Impact Indicators for Adaptation. The methodology for calculating the impact indicators is described in Section D.3.

### D.2 Parallel shift potential (assumed: 500 years; approximately 1,170 project years)

The parallel shift potential of this intervention is required to ensure a future in which resilient ecosystems support adaptive livelihoods. The GCF project will lead to a paradigm shift in natural resource management and the development of climate-resilient agricultural systems that are more productive and sustainable for smallholder farmers. The approach to developing value chains for climate resilient agricultural and tree products, combined with comprehensive management and implementation shifts across the project’s three components, will provide new opportunities for smallholder farmers to increase their income from climate-resilient agriculture and employment and income opportunities for smallholder farmers, and benefits of climate resilience for all project stakeholders. The project will also contribute to a paradigm shift in land use and landscape management by side-by-side with forest landscape restoration by introducing a wider variety of financial products and tools to measure carbon sequestration and other natural resources used under Outputs 1.4, 1.5 & G4 emission reduction from KCS delivered under Output 1.5.

### Contribution to enabling environments: The targeted interventions are proven and validated measures (see section 7 of the Feasibility Study) that contribute to enabling environment for climate resilience through systematically addressing barriers to land management, including:

- **Restoration of degraded lands**: This is achieved by implementing a combination of agroforestry, forest and silvopastoral land management to create resilient land management and landscape restoration. Addressing these barriers (as described in section 7) will enable the implementation of measures that increase the capacity of ecosystems to provide hydrological regulation services and improve cross-sectoral coordination and local government capacity.

- **Conversion of highly degraded lands**: This is done by restoring the most degraded land in order to make agroforestry, forest, and silvopastoral land management financially sustainable in the medium and long term. In delivering this component 1 also addresses barriers to land management, including: (a) lack of access to markets for agricultural products; (b) lack of access to land management practices and techniques preventing the long-term transition to restored and productive landscapes; (c) lack of access to finance for agroforestry, forest, and silvopastoral land management; (d) lack of access to information on best practices in land management. By establishing new markets and long-term buyer relations, the project secures long-term contracting of 10,000ha state-owned degraded lands. The project also provides technical assistance to farmers and FMOs to improve their activities. The two-year investment lifetime is considered most appropriate for this analysis and shows favorable returns on investment (ROI) at the same time generating robust medium and long term economic benefits from a social perspective.

The project supports a paradigm shift in key areas: (a) mainstreaming climate resilience, financial and business planning; (b) strengthening individual farmers’ and FMOs will be equipped with better organized and informed (Output 2.1) and in building capacities for business administration, the development of business plans, and the implementation of these plans (Outputs 2.3); (c) mainstreaming climate resilience measures in their businesses/businesses (Outputs 2.2 and 2.4). A key element of this paradigm shift is to ensure that farmers and FMOs are equipped with the skills and knowledge necessary for them to adopt mainstream agri-biomass assessment, and incentivize farmers to employ these methods. The innovations include: 1) a comprehensive climate resilience framework; (b) an integrated approach to climate risk management systems in agri-landing; (c) new loan products for value chains that address climate impact and value chain actors’ needs; (d) improved access to climate advice; (e) improved digital tools for lending and climate information, and (f) adequate tools for risk mitigation.

Farmers and FMOs will be linked to suitable financial products and services (Output 2.3). Component 2 provides a range of financial services that are tailored to the needs of farmers and FMOs in the agricultural value chains and have the financial resources required to add value to the agricultural and tree products derived from land management activities. The project will also provide technical assistance for the development of new products induced by impacts such as prolonged drought and floods. Interventions will enhance the long-term sustainability and economic viability of the project by improving farmer and FMOs’ capital base through savings accumulation and the deployment of financial services. These interventions will be implemented in a way that maximizes the impact on services in the medium term, including savings and loans, by the targeted population. A major existing market failure for smallholder farmers is the lack of access to finance. The project aims to address this by providing grants to be replaced gradually by private sector investments, is key to ensuring sustainability and scalability of the interventions. The project will also provide technical assistance in the development of new products and services through financial intermediaries during the project lifetime. Once financial services are shown to be successful, financial institutions will be encouraged to scale up their operations with support from public and private actors such as farmer organizations and financial institutions. Alongside this, private companies and investors that are willing to provide relevant finance for the interventions will be identified and supported by the project. These providers will eventually be able to provide relevant finance well beyond GCF financial exit. Furthermore.

## Economic co-benefits

Social and economic benefits will be derived with the introduction of restoration and sustainable land-use practices with positive effects on livelihoods in the Eastern Province, including:

- Improved food security for approximately 376,400 people (256,252 people) and increased productivity and incomes through improved land, soil and water conditions;
- Increased access to markets for agricultural products, contributing to increased groundwater resource availability and increased livestock productivity and health;
- Reduced post-harvest losses of crops and livestock due to the introduction of technologies for processing and marketing of livestock and agricultural goods, improving producers' access to markets, and increasing income from sales.

## Social co-benefits

Social benefits will be delivered throughout the project activities and include:

- Awareness will be raised about climate change effects and adaptation in 556,252 people living in the Eastern Province;
- Delivering capacity building to approximately 150,000 people, with at least 50% representation of women, in a wide range of areas including climate change awareness, livelihoods, and gender equality;
- Create significant social capital through co-designing and managing a range of adaptation strategies. The project will engage women in project planning, investment and decision making from the start.
- Additionally, the project will result in health and nutritional improvement for 126,433 families (556,252 people);
- Increase in crop diversity will reduce exposure of 100,000 families (440,000people) to the risks of climate change;
- Farmers will benefit from increased social cohesion created through working into associations/cooperative associations and a gender equality system.

The project will result in positive outcomes related to access to resources, improved livelihoods, and income generation opportunities for women. **D. Vulnerability of the area and specific vulnerable groups, including gender aspects**

*Vulnerability of the country and/or specific vulnerable groups, including gender aspects*

With a population density of 470/sq km and an annual population growth rate of 2.7%, Rwanda is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa (UNDP, 2015). Eastern Province is one of the most highly populated areas of the country (29% of total population) with a high proportion of young people (48%). The province has a high prevalence of poverty and poor health conditions and social vulnerability. The province has the high rates of poverty (36.5%) and food insecurity (19.2%) of households in Rwanda. This is due to the low levels of access to land, water resources, education, health services, physical and financial resources required for adaptation. More than 80% of rural households own less than 1 ha of land and more than half of them are women-headed.

In the project area, women are especially vulnerable as they traditionally manage household water and family gardens and are thus on the frontline of managing and facing the impacts of reduced water availability and crop failure. This poses a threat to food security and nutrition for their families and communities in the face of climate change and increased droughts. Further information regarding women’s vulnerability to climate change is presented in Annex 8.

*Vulnerable farmers in the areas targeted by the project are at great risk of being pushed into conditions of extreme poverty and hunger, as well as facing a high risk of food insecurity due to reduced water availability and crop failure. The lack of coordinated governance. Land in the Eastern Province is primarily used for farming and grazing (72.3%) and only 18% is forested land. The majority of the population lives on small plots of land, with an average plot size of 0.5 ha. 324,128ha (40 %) are considered very degraded due to inappropriate land management exacerbated by climate change. This has led to a high level of soil erosion and reduced water availability. The lack of access to water for their food insecurity. Climate change forecasts indicate that the Eastern Province will be the region suffering greatest heat stress in Rwanda, with temperatures expected to increase by 2°C over the next two decades. The loss of forest cover reduce the landscape’s capacity to regulate the hydrological cycle. The baseline scenario will result in an average annual temperature rise of 1.5°C and a reduction in rainfall of up to 30%.*

*The project interventions have been designed to meet the needs of recipient beneficiaries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, including increased water scarcity and food insecurity. This section provides information on how to address. For more information on the selection methodology for beneficiaries see Section 6 of the Feasibility Study (Annex 8).*

## Need for strengthening institutions and implementing capacity

The gaps in coordination mechanisms are a constraint to sustainable land management through ecosystem restoration. The lack of institutional arrangements at national, provincial, district and local levels has hindered the development of a common approach to adaptation at a landscape scale. As identified by the National Adaptation Plan (NAP), there is a need for strengthening institutions and implementing capacity and the current institutional arrangement and capacity of the national and local governments, which requires support in terms of human resources, financial resources and technical expertise. The lack of coordination and shortage of institutional technical knowledge and capacity know-how about proven climate risks and solutions. There are also gaps in the institutional arrangements at district level to ensure that the project is implemented. In the absence of the project, furthermore, district governments have no way of self-funding given their limited income streams available for development projects. The lack of a clear land tenure system and weak institutions at national and local levels conditions to ensure natural ownership ensuring districts play a key role in implementing TREEDA on ground both in terms of implementation and monitoring and evaluation. This is also a constraint to the long-term sustainability of this project. There will be project implementation team at each district mostly to manage activities.

The Lead Implementing Entity will be responsible for ensuring districts are fully engaged, project is integrated to the district plans and involved in mid-day monitoring of performance. Each district has a strong Agriculture and Livelihoods Committee (ALC) that can provide technical support to communities and help them deliver outputs. The project will provide additional staffing needed to support implementation in close collaboration with the ALCs and other stakeholders, including local private sector and CSOs to support mobilization and education of communities in line with the project.


### Absence of alternative sources of financing

Rwanda is one of the countries that has some of the highest rates of inequality and one of the worst rates of poverty and malnutrition in the region (39%). Public as well as private investment is essential to overcome these problems. However, Rwanda’s fiscal space is limited due to its high population growth rate relative to the size of its economy. A number of barriers remain to finally attract farmers to understand the benefits of reforestation and agroforestry practices. The project will provide a financial incentive for smallholder farmers by providing them with access to credit at concessional rates, in addition to conventional commercial finance. Given this situation and that climate-responsive financing is not an urgent priority from the government’s perspective, it is unlikely that there would be sufficient public sector funding or liquidity for small-holder farmer investments; the most vulnerable populations have few opportunities for effective savings.

Agriculture is a key sector with a vision of having a productive, green and market-led agriculture sector. The project targets directly the four key pillars of the PESTAG criteria: (1) enabling environment & responsive institutions; (2) productive and sustainable land use management; (3) climate change adaptation and mitigation; and (4) innovation and empowerment. The project has also worked with the Ministry of Environment and Forestry to develop a National Forest Landscape Restoration Strategy, which was approved by the Cabinet on 7 June 2019. The updated policy contains a number of new provisions to better align with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 15 on life on land, as well as other international commitments including the EAC Vision 2050, African Union Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Strategy for Climate Change and Loss Carbon D. The project will contribute to these efforts by directly resulting in 45,000 ha agroforestry, reforestation and forest landscape restoration activities on degraded lands, as well as the creation of a new Forest Landscape Restoration monitoring system aligned with and built on two existing monitoring systems: the District Forest monitoring information system (DFMIS) which has already been developed and now contains 125 sites, and the Community Monitoring Information System which is connected with the District one.

The project's Forest Landscape Restoration monitoring system is aligned with and will build on two existing monitoring systems: the District Forest monitoring information system (DFMIS), which has already been developed and now contains 125 sites, and the Community Monitoring Information System which is connected with the District one.

### Existing GCF country programme

The current GCF country programme targets forest management through restoration and protection of natural forests, afforestation and agroforestry. Also prioritized in the country programme are distribution of high-quality forestation seeds, training on sustainable land use practices, capacity building for community-based forest management (CBFM), climate change adaptation and mitigation, crop diversification and intercropping (training and supply of climate resilient seed varieties), optimized livestock production systems, agroforestry, and integrated soil fertility management. The country programme also includes trainings on sustainable intensification. The existing GCF project: Strengthening climate resilience of rural communities through forest landscape restoration and community-based forest management aims to increase the capacity of communities to restore and sustainably manage forest resources and support smallholders for agroforestry, while increasing the capacity of communities to adapt to climate change. The project targets 10 districts and highly vulnerable communities in the Eastern Province. The project will be implemented through four components:

(1) Communities supported to restore and sustainably manage forest resources; (2) Communities supported to improve sustainable forest management and adopt fuel-efficient cooking methods; (3) Settlements development, including improved water supply; and (4) Successful adaptation and mitigation strategies developed and maintained at the national level.

While this project proposal to GCF focuses on a different geographic area - with specific adaptation needs through land restoration and agroforestry - lessons from the Eastern Province will be applied during implementation of the project in the Eastern Province. The project will significantly leverage FP 07 Green Growth experience through various mechanisms including:

## Role of National Designated Authority (NDA)

The NDA is the Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) due to the high climate sensitivity of the Eastern Province. Selection of IUCN as the FSC was made by REMA.

### How decision-making responsibility related to implementation will be placed with in-country institutions and how domestic systems will be used to ensure accountability

The Project Steering Committee (PSC) will be established at the national level. The PSC will be composed of local institutions both public, private sector and civil society. The current proposed members of PSC include: Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning, Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA), Rwanda Forest Development Authority (RFDA), Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB), Ministry of Infrastructure - Energy department, and Rwanda Water Board (RWB). Other potential members are the National Forestry Commission (NFC), Rwanda Forest Research Institute (RFRI), Civil society organizations (CICD), Rwanda Youth Alliance for Climate Action (Rwanda YACA), community representatives, private sector, etc. The PSC will be chaired by REMA and will include representatives from all sectors including public, private sector. This will enable strategic ownership of the in-country institutions as well as benefiting from this diverse representation.

It is expected that at District level, a district project coordination committee will be established. This will manage day to day implementation activities within each district. The PSC will provide overall guidance and oversight for the project; the project will be integrated as part of District plans from the beginning and will form part of their district's performance contract.

Please describe the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed project/programme, taking into account the MCF financing and mitigation/adaptation impact the project/programme aims to achieve, and explain how this compares to international best practice.

An economic analysis of the project was performed to assess the net incremental benefits the project yields for society. The economic analysis compares costs and benefits in the counterfactual (business-as-usual scenario where no project is implemented) against the actual scenario (where the project is implemented).

The analysis considers two types of benefits: (1) marketable benefits that come from avoiding climate change related losses and increasing production in climate-resilient agricultural systems, and (2) non-market benefits that result from the provision of ecosystem services as a result of project activities. The financial rate of return is calculated separately for each major intervention in Component 1. The measures are ranked according to their expected economic returns over the project period. The costs and benefits are calculated based on the activities undertaken in the same geographic areas in the baseline scenario.

Note also the contribution made by the activities in Components 2 and 3 to the success of Component 1. In particular, Component 2 provides a market for the products produced under Component 1. Similarly, the activities in Component 3 project aims to diversify and enhance the variety of financial services for farmers engaged in different project components.

The financial rate of return is calculated separately for each major intervention in Component 1. The measures are ranked according to their expected economic returns over the project period. The costs and benefits are calculated based on the activities undertaken in the same geographic areas in the baseline scenario.

Financial returns are calculated (1) assuming business-as-usual, (2) assuming the project investments are made directly by farmers without external support, and (3) assuming GCF support and co-financing. Note that scenarios (2) is not a realistic assumption as it does not take into account the enabling environment for farmers to implement these measures independently, perhaps by taking out commercial loans, when there is no evidence of this happening in the baseline scenario. Scenario 1 assumes that all project investments are made directly by farmers and is the case of what is possible without GCF support.

The discount rate was chosen from the private perspective using a discount rate of 15.28%. This rate was chosen by using the most recent documented interest rate on bank deposits (12%) and multiplying it by 2 to reflect


---

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.0 | PAGE 79 OF 119

inherent risks of agricultural activities. While most loans to farmers will have a tenure between 1-5 years, this financial analysis considers the full life of agroforestry and other landscape restoration investments. The discount rate is set at 15% per year. This means that an investment with a net present value (NPV) greater than USD 100 over 20 years has a net present value of less than USD 6 using the 15% discount rate in this analysis.

The financial analysis for Output 1.1 (agroforestry) evaluates the costs and benefits of resilient agroforestry-based land restoration versus business as usual (BAU). The GCF investment case yields a lower per-hectare NPV than BAU, but it has a higher IRR. This means that the NPV for the GCF investment case is negative over 10 years and becomes higher than BAU after 10 and 20 years as the long-lived agroforestry investments bear fruit; for agroforestry investments, this is reflected in revenues. The simple payback time for the additional up-front investments in the GCF TREP scenario is 6 years.

## Note also that the forest restoration activities described in Output 1.2 generate large and positive externalities beyond ensuring sustainable livelihoods for farmers.

- Increased resilience of the woodlands to climate impacts through sustainable forest management practices.
- Improved climate resiliency of forests which will reduce topsoil erosion, improve water quality, protect source watersheds, and provide ample water supply for households needs (Drinking and Irrigation) (Wilson and Love, 2016; Gantay et al., 2014).
- Reduced stormwater runoff resulting in flood risk mitigation (e.g. Mathews et al. 2004; Ramon et al. 2004).
- Increased biodiversity.

These benefits, while significant, are not captured by the farmers who restore the forests and collect wood and are therefore not included in the financial cost-benefit analysis.

In each climate resilience scenario, GCF investment makes the project interventions more financially attractive for farmers. Long-term financial returns are positive and the financial returns were significant without GCF support. GCF support provides incentives for long-term sustainability beyond the implementation phase.

Finally, the financial analysis is used in Output 1.5 to identify the technological interventions that will be used to reduce the use of biomass fuel for cooking and thus reduce reliance on climate sensitive forest resources. The investment in improved stoves and other technologies will also help to meet the growing demand for fuelwood and thereby reduce the demand-supply imbalance that must be addressed by the on-farm resource management activities. The financial analysis is used as a tool to identify the most cost-effective interventions is qualitatively different than for the on-farm resilience activities. Here, the BAU scenario is continued until 2039 with no investment in improved stoves and other technologies. This is because the demand for wood stoves, with subsidies provided only for the poorest households. Affordability is ensured by facilitating access to short term credit, buttressed by the financial and time savings that come from adoption of ICCS.

| 4+ year old wood stove (daily/longer use) | 125,000 | - |
| 2-year old wood stove (daily/longer use) | 90,000 | - |
| 3 years old wood stove (daily/longer use) | 100,000 | - |
| LPG Stove | 250,000 | - |
| Bio-Catalytic briquette | 200,000 | - |
| Electric stove (no ICS) | 350,000 | - |

Since most households will have to make the investment themselves, simple payback period is the critical financial measure for this analysis. The results identify four stove types where the initial investment plus ongoing fuel costs make financial sense for unsubsidized households, meaning they will recoup their initial investment within the lifetime of the stove. These stoves are the 3-year old wood stove (frequent/brief use), 4+ year old wood stove (daily/longer use) promoted by the project because poor households would never recoup their initial investment based on typical usage patterns.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.0 | PAGE 88 OF 119

ICCN: Enabling IUCN/ICNAF will introduce a series of climate resilient agriculture practices, including silvopastoralism, agroforestry, forest landscape restoration. The project will build on a range of lessons learned and best practices from the pilot projects in the Eastern Province, ROAM, village land use plans, and other resilient land use practices already piloted.

The following is a list of some of the key technologies and approaches that are being adopted:

- Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) for adaptation to future climate.
- Tree fodder, grasses and herbaceous leguminous production for improving milk production and restore degraded lands.
- Biomass incorporation from fertilizer trees for improving soil fertility.
- Establishment of agroforestry systems in the Eastern Province and in seedling business production.
- Improved silvopastoral systems (e.g. paddocking and innovative fodder conservation for increased resilience).
- Water supply through Rain water harvesting and boreholes without destabilize ground water.
- Climate-smart livestock production on farms.
- Clean and efficient cooking technologies.
- Inclusive financial instruments for climate resilient value chains, and
- Cross-sectoral planning and community landscape restoration planning.

### Main Output 1: Priority landscapes brought under restoration to support climate resilient agro-ecological systems and livelihoods in Eastern Province.

**139** Published Landscape Restoration Plans within annual district development strategies must include landscape restoration plans and improved incentives for investment in long-term agroforestry, afforestation and forestry restoration activities by private sector foresters (Government of Kenya, 2018). The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) is a global forest certification system that provides an international standard which establishes a number of objective criteria to evaluate the capacity of district governments and evaluate the seven cross-sectoral planning and implementation strategies. These include: 1) degree of integrating climate resilience metrics, 2) presence of annual performance contracts, 3) degree of harmonizing cross-sectoral investments, 4) degree of integration with other sectoral plans, 5) degree of inclusion of gender equality and social equity in restoration activities for participation of men and women and marginalised groups, and 4) contribute to coherent reporting at all governance level.

## 5.1.4 Provide technical assistance to farmers to support them on the implementation of agroforestry practices, including tree planting and seedling production and distribution.

### 5.1.4.1 Technical assistance to farmers for tree planting and seedling production and distribution.
The project will provide free tree seeds and saplings to farmers in the targeted areas.

#### 5.1.4.2 Technical assistance to train farmers on agroforestry practices, including tree planting and seedling production and distribution.
Special attention will be given to training women and youth farmers on agroforestry practices, including tree planting and seedling production and distribution.

#### 5.1.4.3 Technical assistance to provide technical support for the management of fruit trees which will maximize the production of fruits and other agricultural products in the project area.
The project will provide technical support for the management of fruit trees which will maximize the production of fruits and other agricultural products in the project area.

#### 5.1.4.4 Technical assistance to train farmers on the selection, planting, and care of agroforestry crops that will ensure the full success.
Advice on crop selection, planting, and care will be provided by extension workers or local experts who can provide it as facilitators.

### 5.1.5 Establish and sustain 1 demonstration plot of 1-2 ha in each of the 100 sub-districts.

#### 5.1.5.1 For each of the targeted 300 sub-districts, establish a demonstration plot of at least 1-2 ha which will be used as a model for other farmers.
The project will establish and sustain one demonstration plot of 1-2 ha in each of the 100 sub-districts.

#### 5.1.5.2 Establish framing contract with local authorities for maintenance of demonstration plots.
The project will establish framing contracts with local authorities for maintaining the demonstration plots.

#### 5.1.5.3 Organize training and workshops on agroforestry practices, including tree planting and implementation etc.
Training and workshops on agroforestry practices, including tree planting and implementation etc., will be organized to train farmers in the project area.

### 5.1.6 Monitoring, control and evaluation of supported agroforestry areas

#### 5.1.6.1 Collect and register information on the status of agroforestry plots.
Significant data were recorded and registered in the agroforestry database for each plot (e.g., location, area, tree species, etc.) and specifically designed software will be used to collect this information.

#### 5.1.6.2 Collect and register information on the status of facilitators.
The project will collect and register information on the status of facilitators (i.e., the registration for each facilitator, including their name, address, phone number, etc.).

#### 5.1.6.3 Collect and register information on the status of plots per species, the planting date, and the status of the agroforestry plot.
The project will collect and register information on the status of plots per species, the planting date, and the status of the agroforestry plot.

Design of SFM of district owned forests for sustainable management and use.

#### 5.2.1.2 Support district land managers to implement forest laws, policies, and strategies.

### 2.2.1: Tree-crop value chain development

#### Key to sustainable supply of tree crops is the development of private sector enterprises and community-managed tree seed systems, established to secure the supply of high-quality seeds and planting material at affordable numbers in support of restoration efforts beyond this activity. ## E.T. Monitoring, reporting and evaluation arrangements (max. 500 words; approximately 1 page)

Besides the arrangements (e.g., annual performance reports) laid out in ARA, please give a summary of the project/programme specific arrangements for monitoring and evaluation. Please provide the types of interim and final evaluations that will be conducted during the life of the project/programme. The arrangements should also include the process for reporting to the GCF Board and/or the GCF Secretariat as well as any other relevant reporting obligations between AE and Executing Entity (EE) as relevant, including reporting obligations from the EE to the AE. This includes the frequency of reporting.

The activities on monitoring, action learning, evaluation and reporting are incorporated Component 3. SBCN will lead this activity through the development and implementation of a monitoring, evaluation, and reporting (MERL) strategy and plan. The process for monitoring, action learning, evaluation and reporting and evaluation system are outlined below and managed by project actors in the inception phase.

### Monitoring

The monitoring activities measure the expected results, indicators, means of verification, baseline values and target values at mid-term and end-term.

#### (a) Data collection, management and reporting system: A fit-for-purpose data collection, management and reporting system will be developed to ensure that all project/programme data is collected, managed and reported throughout the life of the programme. The annual/semi-annual reports will provide information on the performance of the project/programme against its objectives and indicators. Reports will include a summary of progress towards achieving results, evidence of success during the reporting period, constraints during implementation and how they were addressed. Reporting will also include an assessment of the effectiveness of monitoring and evaluation management to respond to needs. Reports will also include a compilation of lessons learned, adaptive management, and any other relevant information that may be useful for future projects. The data collection system will use existing technology particularly for forestry and agroforestry management proposed under component 1.

#### (b) Methodology and tools: Monitoring project results, project managers and independent assessors will utilise various tools and methodologies to collect and report on the progress of project activities against indicators. These include:

- **Participatory Rapid Rural Appraisal (PRA)**: A participatory tool for assessing the status of Land Degradation and Sustainable Land Management in Grassland and Pastoral Systems.
- **Stakeholder Approach to Risk Assessment**: A risk assessment methodology developed by SRI, IUCN, and WETNET. These tools are used to identify risks and uncertainties (RUs) and user friendly decision support systems (DSS).
- **GIS**: A tool for data collection and analysis that can be used as a decision-making tool.
- **Socio-economic surveys**: A tool to collect baseline socio-economic data and land use information.

The main methodological approaches will include:

- Participatory rapid rural assessments, combined with remote sensing to specifically monitor cover area covered by rehabilitation activities.
- Regular fieldsite monitoring visits to document and validate the number and coverage of ecosystem-based interventions (EBIs) in terms of their impact on biodiversity and ecosystem services.
- Knowledge, Attitude and Practice (KAP) survey to monitor programme beneficiaries.
- Scorecards to assess degree of awareness and integration of climate change to national sector plans; and
- Vulnerability assessments to monitor changes in adaptive capacity and reduced exposure to climate risks.

## Social risks related to potential people equity and access to project benefits, including:

- Risk of unjustified preferential treatment when selecting sites and beneficiaries of project services.
- Risk of discrimination or unjustified preferential treatment when choosing farmers as promoters/facilitators and who would benefit from the project.
- Risk of excluding gender groups through design of training measures (e.g. timing of training, composition of training groups).
- Risk of unjustified preferential treatment in case owner of the plots will receive benefits and as such would have an unfair advantage over other farmers.
- Risk of impacting vulnerable groups whose livelihood depend on forest resources or on biomass resources from the buffer zones.
- Potential risk of discrimination or preferential treatment when selecting the FMCs that will benefit from project services and resources.
- Potential risk of discrimination or preferential treatment when distributing tree seedlings.
- Potential risk of discrimination or preferential treatment when distributing water tanks and constructing troughs.
- Risk of unjustified preferential treatment in case of the distribution of the IRCS (p.m. per credit or subsidy).

## Mitigation Measures

Through in-depth consultations with communities and stakeholders during the proposal development process and throughout project implementation, and through the engagement of community leaders, this project will ensure that no one is left behind. The project will also ensure that women are not discriminated against when it comes to training, youth, elders and women in targeted communities. A rigorous methodology for beneficiaries' selection is in place to ensure that all groups have equal access to project services. Equal representation of men and women will be taken in training activities. In relevant activities, the Ubuntuwe social categorization will be taken into consideration, ensuring that no group is discriminated against or left behind. The Ubuntuwe Social Categorization Committee periodically ranks the households in their area on a scale of 1 to 6 according to their perceived poverty and vulnerability status. This ranking will be used as an indicator for project beneficiaries selection. In addition, the needs of each group is appropriately taken into consideration. Where appropriate, the project will make use of traditional dispute resolution mechanisms such as gbaca and abusa.

More details on mitigation of social risks are provided in the ESMF.

### Mitigation Measures

The project aims to build the resilience in the Eastern Province by increasing the adaptive capacity of men and women in the Eastern Province. The risk of not having adequate operational capacity has been identified through project design and planning, and the various initiatives involved have considered this as a potential risk. This risk is being managed by ensuring that all project activities are aligned with the Ministry’s priorities and objectives. The risk of this capacity not being available is considered low, given that all project plans are clearly aligned with the Ministry's priorities and objectives. However, the levels of support required will be continually monitored and adjusted through the project's M&E system. In the unlikely event that the operational capacity falls short, it can be addressed through cross-sectoral project governance system, reflecting the shared responsibility for the success of the project.

The project does not include any activities that require physical displacement (resettlement) or involuntary taking of land (land acquisition). However, there is a possibility that restoration measures implemented in the three land use systems will result in restrictions on access to land. The project will ensure that these restrictions are minimal and temporary.

Agakusa National Park might require new access restrictions or strengthening enforcement of existing access restrictions. This may affect the livelihoods of vulnerable people who depend directly on the park for collection of woodlots and tree plantations and through elevated supply capacities bring down costs for woody biomass and as such, reduce their income. The project will ensure that these restrictions are minimal and temporary.

The project will also ensure that any access restrictions to land use systems in the buffer zone of Agakusa National Park are minimal and temporary. In case of permanent restrictions on the use of forest and resources are required: this might affect the livelihoods of vulnerable people who depend directly on the park for collection of woodlots and tree plantations.

In case of permanent restrictions, if this is not sufficient to restore their livelihoods, the requirement to provide additional livelihood support will be addressed in Annex 5 of the ESMR.

# Mitigation Measure(s)

Table 20 in the FS lists the species that have been pre-selected for the agroforestry systems and in Annex I the FS provides a list of species that are not recommended to be planted as they may pose risks of developing invasive characteristics. The project will continue with Eucalyptus or acacia species as these are already there and focus on effective management of existing poorly managed forests including establishing new markets and long-term contracts for timber, wood products and non-timber forest products (NTFPs). These include the establishment of moisture, light availability, fire regimes, nitrogen mineralization rates and soil pH. It is not intended to introduce exotic species in areas where native species are already present or where there is a risk of developing invasive characteristics.

For forest restoration, the project will continue with Eucalyptus or acacia species as these are already there and focus on effective management of existing poorly managed forests including establishing new markets and long-term contracts for timber, wood products and non-timber forest products (NTFPs). These include the establishment of moisture, light availability, fire regimes, nitrogen mineralization rates and soil pH. It is not intended to introduce exotic species in areas where native species are already present or where there is a risk of developing invasive characteristics.

Regarding the risk on water competition from the use of Eucalyptus, it has to be noted that the use of Eucalyptus will be restricted only to restore existing very degraded Eucalyptus small-leafed woodlot (6543) ha = 0.7% of the EP land area and not for new plantings. The establishment of these woodlots is expected to have a positive impact on water availability, significantly the sustainable supply capacity of wood, the carbon sequestration, the restoration of forest ecosystem services and the reduction in fire risk (e.g., by reducing the amount of fine fuel available). However, the establishment of farming contracts with sawmillwood pellet companies will contribute to the reduction of fire risk. The project will also establish a firebreak network to mitigate the risk on water competition. Also, most of the tree plantations are located on the uprisen areas of water catchment on slopes > 10% and therefore have no direct impact on water availability.

In consequence, risk of competing with crops for groundwater resources is very limited. Anyway, to mitigate any minor risk of competition between Eucalyptus and crops, it will be recommended to establish the plantations in areas where they use less water, while applying silviculture techniques (longer coppice period, avoid removal of leaves and small branches, etc.). The project will also support the restoration/improvement of forest ecosystem services (soil erosion and fertility control, water regulation).

Firebreaks are used only in a few areas where fire risk exists, especially nearby shrubland of Kirehe, Gasabo and Nyamagabe Districts. These firebreaks have been established to reduce the risk of fire spread from agricultural land by climate change impact itself. This fire risk is usually and systematically mitigated by the establishment of firebreaks, as well as by the adoption of good silviculture practices with good forest coverage limiting small dry grasses that could support the propagation.

G. GCF POLICIES AND STANDARDS

### G.1 Environmental and social risk assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.6 pages)

The project was designed considering the potential social and environmental risks and impacts as well as IUCN's relevant safeguard standards. The proposal has been screened on social and environmental risks following the procedures described in the Project Design Document (PDD) and the Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP). It is being classified as a moderate risk project (category B). The detailed results of the ESMS screening and the rationale for this classification are presented below.

The project is expected to lead to positive environmental and social impacts as its aim is to transform drought-degraded land in the Eastern Province into restored, productive, and climate-resilient ecosystems. In addition to environmental benefits, the project will also improve livelihood conditions through enhanced ecosystem services relevant for local communities. The project has been designed with a focus on ensuring that all stakeholders are involved from the outset: holders and households – including energy-efficient cooking stoves and new income opportunities associated with the restoration of degraded land. However, there is a risk that these benefits may not be realized if the environmental risks are not managed effectively.

The key risks and mitigation strategies are described below. It is not expected, however, that any of them will materialize as they are all low in likelihood and/or severity. The project has been categorized as moderate risk because it affects sensitive receptors (biodiversity, humans etc.), that were diverse, unpredictable, irreversible or permanent. Most of the risk issues are judged as low risks, one only is a moderate one and it is expected that the low risk issues can be managed effectively through good management practices and mitigation measures. The project in this therefore categorized as moderate risk project.

While the geographical focus of the project has been defined as the Eastern Province and it seven districts, the target landscape for restoration is the entire area within the buffer zone of the Akaara National Park. This selection was based on the climate vulnerability of the sites based on exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity; state of ecosystem degradation as well as respective physical and socio-economic drivers for degradation. This analysis is guided by the ESMP (table 4) which presents a risk assessment matrix that identifies risks and their likelihoods. As a consequence, a more detailed risk analysis will be undertaken once the sites have been selected and the restoration and rehabilitation activities are defined.

The Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) for this project has been prepared in accordance with IUCN’s ESMP guidelines (see attachment 6). It has consequently been prepared (see attachment 60) that delineates the process of assessing risks and identifying suitable mitigation measures and spells out requirements for consultation and disclosure.

A high-level assessment of environmental and social risks has been carried out based on the general interventions described in Full Proposal. The Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) has been presented in the ESMP (table 4) assessing the significance of the identified risks based on estimated likelihood of occurrence and impact, as well as the potential for mitigation measures to reduce these risks or enhance positive measures. Because the final location of the activities and related context-specific details are not yet known, the table is left to be understood as indicative. Its purpose is to provide general guidance for the detailed design of the interventions.

The key environmental and social risks and impacts and the measures on how the project will avoid, minimize and mitigate negative impacts are presented below:

Risks from temporary use restrictions: The project will face the restoration measures on three land-use systems, (i) agriculture; (ii) forest and woodland; and (iii) degraded land and shrublands areas owned by the State and (iv) in the buffer zone of the Akaara National Park which is under joint management authority of the Rwanda Development Board and African Parks Network. While the restoration and forest management practices are expected to increase the productivity of these lands, they may also lead to temporary use restrictions on land that is currently used for traditional biomass and as such household expenditures in particular for cooking fuel; for restoration measures to be effective, often a period of time will be required before the benefits can be realized. This could have negative impacts on vulnerable people who are highly dependent on these forest resources and display a low adaptive capacity. To identify, avoid and address livelihood impacts from access restrictions a Process Framework (PF) has been developed in

### G.2 Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately |1 page)

#### G.2.1 Gender assessment and action plan (see annex 8)
IUCN undertook a gender assessment based on community consultations and statistical analysis to identify principal gender-related constraints in the agricultural sector of the Province of Rwanda. In Rwanda women constitute 65% of the agricultural work force, however only 19.7% of men are paid for their labor. The study concluded that women have limited access to land which would enhance their capacity to adapt to climate change—including food, credit, agricultural inputs, decision-making technology and training services. Women's coping mechanisms to climate change are still limited due to high poverty, low literacy rates, limited access to extension services and different cultural norms: traditional roles, and power


---
**Page 121**
---

relations between men and women. Findings highlight women’s limited mobility outside their homes (1) in the case of hunger/famine due to prolonged drought, women and children are the most affected, because they move in search of food or money and can come back home even after one or two months.

As women are key players in the agricultural sector this project seeks to address the situation. Thus, Men and Women will be involved in the design and implementation of all components and indicators. About 20% of the households in the project area are female-headed households. At least 220,132 women in the project area will benefit from alternative income opportunities and the implementation of climate resilient agriculture technologies and value chain linkages. Approximately 250,131 women will benefit from skills development and access to extension services.

The design of the project integrates gender sensitive planning and implementation, particularly for women farmers and women-headed households. The project will also ensure that women are involved in all aspects of the project through responsive and transformative tools. The project seeks to improve the access for women to the benefits from agroforestry and silvopastoral systems as well as sustainable energy resources while enhancing women opportunities for income generation.

Component 1 supports female population by increased capacities for implementing resilient forest land use management through agroforestry and silvopastoral systems to strengthen food security and use of improved conservation practices. The component will also support the implementation of the Gender Action Plan (GAP) which address the specific needs of women (especially indigenous women) and enable them to be risk informed and adopt resilient agricultural practices to secure food even in drought periods. Outcomes from Component 2 include increased access for women to alternative income opportunities, improved livelihoods and enterprises that generate additional income as well as increased access to sustainable finance and business development support. In particular, the project will provide training on agroforestry and silvopastoral systems to women farmers in the face of climate related shocks caused by drought. Other proposed diversified activities particularly focus on opportunities for women such as managing seed nurseries and adopting agroforestry systems.

In addition, project actions will be developed in alignment with the Vision 2030 strategy, which emphasizes that gender equality is one of the key pillars of the strategy. This will ensure that the project contributes to the achievement of Vision 2030 and hence Vision’s goal.
