With a trained farmer promoter in every village, all farmers in Rwanda will have local access to an extension agent. As the level of technical knowledge in every village improves, crop yields and quality increase along with household incomes.

Notwithstanding the fact that farmer promoters are very instrumental in the dissemination of extension services, agricultural good practices and technology innovations, again women are not well represented in this platform. In all the four agricultural zones, women represent their colleagues on these platforms are between 12 percent (the lowest being Eastern Province) to 16 percent (the highest being Southern Province). Given this situation, Eastern Province needs attention. The following were the reasons for women underrepresentation, per the findings from the FGDs conducted with women and men in Kayonza District:

- One fundamental reason is the low access of women to information about agricultural services, which is a consequence of their limited participation in meetings with government extension agents. Hence, men tend to meet and share information about agriculture extension services and about the farmer promoter system with peer men, so that information rarely reaches women.
- The second factor is related to social status. In general, being part of the farmer promoters is regarded by many villagers as an elevation to a higher social status giving them more exposure in their villages. This social status prompt men to jump to the opportunity, especially given their position as head of families.
- The third reason relates to opportunities associated with farmer promoters' activities, such as training opportunities, participation in study tours, etc. Men tend to make sure that they are at the front of such initiatives so that they can benefit from these opportunities. The absence


---
**Page 286**
---

of affirmative actions at policy level to promote equitable participation of men and women among farmer promoters can be highlighted as a key factor that explains the above-mentioned gaps.

• Another factor mentioned is the limited time of women farmers in rural areas to engage in extra-farm activities. Being overburdened with the labour-intensive work of agriculture in addition to their usual household chores and other unpaid work, women find it difficult to dedicate time to community development activities, such as the farmer promoters.


## Farmer Field Schools (FFS)

In a bid to help smallholder farmers, the ministry for agriculture and animal resources introduced a learning farm system called farmer field school since 2013. Also known in Twangamwe as "kiburi ry'Abahinda mu Muungano", FFS is implemented through a learning practical scenario where the plant symbolizes a teacher; the field is the school itself and the farmer, the learner. The initiative was made decentralized at the village level, employing best-trained farmers who teach their neighbours using their own best fields (Elias Hakizimana, 2017).


Introduced in Rwanda since 2009, Farmer Field School is a participatory extension approach in which selected farmers are trained to become facilitators. The FFS approach impacts on farming practices on major crops such as maize and beans by disseminating information on harvesting techniques, planting and organizing workers in a bid to increasing productivity. It also helps in integrating research in the field as well as continuously looking for innovations in agriculture. Participatory agricultural extension approaches include elements of participatory development in that it enables farmers to participate in problem-solving processes and decision-making. Farmers are encouraged to choose those technologies that are adapted to their specific challenges, and validate adopted technologies.


Cultural norms limit women's ability to participate in and access training programs, including farmer field days and demonstration events. This inability to learn about new agricultural technologies, seeds, and technologies leads to lower productivity for women farmers. Improving access to these resources and programs involves changing ways that tradition and culture hold women back. For example, training is often held at times when men are away from home or during the day when women are at school (USAID, 2015:14) As of 2014, Rwanda Agriculture Board identified 44 FFS Master Trainers and 2,547 FFS Facilitators countrywide who work with 96,856 Farmers organized in 3,912 FFS groups.

With more women now better engaged in farming activities, there is need to increase their engagement in extension services.

It is expected that FFS Master Trainers will play a big role in streamlining the FFS extension approach in Rwanda, especially under the new Twigi extension model, a nationally adopted holistic approach in decentralizing extension services to the village level, and meant to empower agricultural promoters living daily with farmers. At the level of FFS Facilitators (those that has successfully completed a season-long training course on topics such as disease management, crop harvesting, training and organizing workers), data from the Rwanda Agriculture Board show there are 2,437 FFS Facilitators spread over four agro-ecological zones as of December 2014.

Women make enormous contributions to the agricultural value chain and household food security through labour on the farm and in home gardens that often goes unrecognized in national statistics (MINAGRI, 2010). However, their access to training opportunities are limited for several reasons. Women headed households including households chores conflict with their ability, household poverty and lack of competing responsibilities are among the key factors that hinder women’s effective participation in agricultural programs such as extension services and trainings (GMO, 2017:16).

Many women also defer to their male spouses, even if the women perform most farm work. Trainers are not required to ensure that an equal number of men and women participate in trainings, and performance is often expressed in numbers of trainers trained, without being disaggregated by sex (MINAGRI, 2010). Most extension staff are men, and they find hard to communicate with


---
**Page 288**
---

male farmers. As a result, there is little incentive to recruit women participants. Training programmes are also often designed without regard to the needs of women with respect to childcare and household duties, among other things.

Agribusiness and agro processing (including SME)

Fewer women than men work in the formal agriculture business, because they face challenges such as the consent of their husbands to engage in business for married women, limited access to the loan services, access and control over land, and a lower level of education as well as technical know-how and access to markets. Women who are engaged in informal small and medium enterprises (SMEs), women entrepreneurs are more likely than their male colleagues involved in the informal sector. Typical activities of women include running smaller firms mainly in service sectors and thus operating in lower value-added sectors. In addition, they operate many home-based businesses than men do.

Rwandan Government supported the establishment of Microfinance Institutions as a way of providing financial accessibility to all Rwandans who cannot afford big loans from the banking institutions especially those engaged in small scale enterprises. The majority of women entrepreneurs in Rwanda SMEs make up approximately 98% of the total business and account for 41% of all private sector employments where women are headed for 42% of enterprises in the country and they comprise 58% of the enterprises in the informal sector that accounts for the 30% of the GDP. Despite microfinance contributions, many female entrepreneurs, like their male counterparts experience many problems in their businesses, which have led to a different mix of constraints including financial credit accessibility, limited share of contracts, access to trade and procurement guidelines and regulatory frameworks. The Microfinance Institutions (MFI) in Rwanda (Rwanda MFIs) is upon the above that is why the researcher would like to establish the extent which Micro Finance contributes to the growth of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs)in Rwanda (Musandamera Laetitia, Jaya Shikha, Anthony Luvanda, 2015:3).

The same study showed that the largest number of establishments in micro- and small-sized enterprises were sole-proprietorships, and that the owners were the sole employee. Around 50 percent of enterprises were sole- proprietorships and around 40 percent were female sole-proprietorships.

**Agriculture technologies**

The government and development partners are increasingly supporting farmers to shift from rain-fed agriculture to irrigated systems. Some of these are commercialized and this will contribute to the increasing of the number of smallholder farmers who are more remunerative employed in agriculture. Irrigated systems also produce high yields, are more reliable, and hence will increase men and women's incomes. The irrigated systems such as marshland for rice production throughout the country or center pivot or sprinkler systems mainly used for maize production in Eastern Province have considerably increased food production and reduced food insecurity in the area, because of either increased yields or more production during season C (the third growing season).


---
**Page 291**
---

The Rwandan government has set a goal to establish irrigation systems on 60,000 hectares of hilly land by 2020. However, men are the most involved in irrigation and water management related activities. Information from FGDs indicates that they spend extra hours putting in place and maintaining irrigation infrastructures, especially during dry seasons. Women mainly perform marginal work to do with irrigation such as physical labor for distributing irrigation systems and other support services. Participants to FGD also indicated that women are not interested in irrigation initiatives, since most of crops cultivated on area under irrigation are not staple crops, which are crucial to local food security.

Presently, marialand irrigation has been developed, while hillside irrigation is newly developed only on a small scale. All marialand and public land managed by the government. Large-scale irrigation and distribution systems have been built and these systems are then lent to farmer associations or cooperatives. The area land under irrigation system has now reached 3 percent of agricultural land (or total land surface!). The government has developed all irrigation infrastructures, and farmers with support of the government have established only a few small-scale irrigation works. Thus, there are no data currently on the owners of farmland under irrigation systems. Use of modern tools (machines) for planting, post-harvesting and other agricultural activities is becoming a common practice in Rwandan agriculture. This may facilitate agriculture activity value chains.

### 3.0 GENDER ACCESS TO FINANCE

The target for the Financial Sector Development Programme (FSDP) was to ensure that 80 percent of the Rwandan population has access to formal financial services by 2017. With respect to financial inclusion, the 2016 FinScope report found that 87 percent of women are financially included as well as 91 percent of men, resulting in a merely low overall gender gap of 4 percent. This is a significant improvement from 2009 and 2012, when financial inclusion was at 26.8 percent and 39 percent, respectively (GMO, 2019: 25). The following table gives the details:

Financial inclusion looked at in terms of proximity and access to formal banking products, services needs to be accelerated to meet female consumers' aspirations. The table above highlights the gender inequality in financial inclusion in Rwanda. Women engage more with informal groups, cooperatives, income-generating groups or other entrepreneurial activities, and community activities. However, for many women in Rwanda, access to credit programs and services is still restricted due to illiteracy, lack of collateral and time issues. Both women and men most commonly use informal credit as a source of finance from family, friends, or local money lender (Country Survey Rwanda 2012:6). With majority of women engaging in borrowing from informal groups, more efforts are needed in addressing women full inclusion.

### 3.8 POWER AND DECISION-MAKING

In addition to being a basic human right, gender equality is increasingly seen as a development catalyst. It is a key role-player in Rwanda’s democracy and integration into the East African Community (EAC). Ensuring women’s participation in governance processes and providing equal access to services are preconditions to facilitate inclusive and effective democratic governance.

Gender equality should not only be recognised on a legal and legislative level, but should be integrated into political, economic, social and cultural strata. Despite formal efforts made to address gender equality, in practice, women and men do not enjoy the same rights and, social, political, economic and other spheres of public life. Gender stereotypes are still part of society and perpetuate gender stereotypes within families, public life, political processes, administrative procedures, and the organisation of society as a whole. However, within these domains, there is also the opportunity to adopt new approaches and initiate change.

The Government of Rwanda (GoR), with the participation of Rwandan women has been pursuing gender equality since 1994. Since then, the participation of Rwandan women has been facilitated by a constitutional mandate and the work of key institutions such as the Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion, the Rwanda Women Parliamentarians Forum (FRRP), National Women’s Council (NWC) and the Government Office (GO). Rwanda’s political parties have created a remarkable political space for themselves in just over 10 years. During the 2013 Rwandan presidential election, a record-breaking 64% of women were elected as women candidates (Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion [MIGEPROF], 2010).


---
**Page 295**
---

In Rwanda, a conscious effort has been made to implement gender-related policies and laws. In its preamble, the Constitution of the Republic of Rwanda of 2003 states that the country is committed to ensuring equal rights for all Rwandans without prejudice, while adhering to the principles of gender equality and complementarity in national development.

### Decision making and governance

Transformational Governance includes the role of men and women and their participation in government decision-making processes to build a secure and stable nation, which provides a platform for economic and social transformation. The Gender constitutional quota of 30% as provided by the Rwandan constitution, combined with a strong political will, gender responsive policies and legal environment as well as enhancement of capacity and mentorship for women led to increased representation of women in decision making organs and improved gender responsiveness of development programmes (GMO, 2019:51).

### Constraints limiting women's participation in decision making

In this section, the consultant documents any cultural, social, legal, and other constraints limiting women’s participation in decision making at the household and community levels, or the use of resources and distribution of project benefits. Opportunities for women’s voices and rights (e.g., participation in village savings and loan associations, projects, and committees; membership in watershed management groups, landscape restoration committees); political empowerment (e.g., local governance structures, leadership training); or access to grievance mechanism(s) will be analysed in this section. Moreover, women's barriers and constraints to full participation in decision-making is highlighted in this section.

Many women are not empowered within their households and need permission from men to access health care. ### 3.9 GENDER ROLES AND TIME USE IN DOMESTIC CONTEXT

By talking about time and space in gender analysis, the concern would like to recognize gender differences in the amount of work and allocation of time as well as the space in which time is spent. It includes the division of both productive and reproductive labor, identifying how time is spent and committed during the day, week, month, or year, and in different settings, and determining how people contribute to the maintenance of the family, community, and society.

#### Division of labour

Women continue to face a "double burden" where their time is taken up with domestic responsibilities such as collection of fuel wood, water, and food. They also use their time for unpaid work like cooking, caring for infants and the elderly, and care for small animals, and they carry out many activities related to production such as paid employment and help on family farms (USAID, 2015:2). The different structural roles of men and women in the market economy are coupled with correspondingly different—and unbalanced—roles in the household economy. In unskilled labour, men dominate in some types of work and women in others. Women's participation in paid employment is often limited by their possessing less physical strength, such as cleaning. Participation in skilled labour such as office work or transformation processes depends on the level of education and experience of both men and women.

Because of unequal gender roles in the household, women have double or even triple the responsibility of men. While men typically work outside the home, women care for children and sick relatives and perform household chores in addition to subsistence farming. Unequal gender roles are considered common in many countries, particularly in rural areas where early marriage is prevalent. Examples of young girls being expected to help their mothers with housework tasks while boys are given more opportunities to play, attend school, or study. Female headed households are at a particular disadvantage since they must fulfill their household responsibilities in addition to earning income to support the family.

The time burden of responsibilities both inside and outside the home can prevent women from accessing health services. They do not have time for long waits in health centers, traveling to distant facilities, or navigating the different steps in the referral process. Informants reported that women usually do not take the time to look after their own health until they are very sick. Additionally, judgement from community members when men perform tasks culturally attributed to women deter men from seeking household services. Conversely, when women are ill or occupied at health facilities Unequal gender roles also affect reporting of SGBV since women fear for their families' wellbeing if men, the main income earners, are condemned (USAID, 2018:4).


---
**Page 299**
---

Gendered division of labour can be observed at all nodes of the value chain; roles are influenced by the production system. In the extensive grazing system that predominates in Nyagatare, for instance, men and boys bring animals to graze and find water, while women mainly care for calves and home processing of milk into butter, cheese, and milk and butter. In the zero-grazing system, which predominates in the rest of Rwanda and is associated with small-scale dairy development projects, women describe the workload is generally heavy, particularly for women, who are responsible for ensuring the cleanliness of utensils and stalls as well as feeding the animals (Umuzurganbeho, 2017:10). Gendered division of labour in agriculture, which remains a major source of income and employment, are still prevalent. Women spend significantly longer time than men on domestic tasks and have less time for leisure and for seeking other work using their new skills, for personal care and for rest (FAO, 2016:22)

In addition to their prominence in agriculture and in the informal sector, women bear the brunt of domestic tasks that are often arduous, time-intensive, and energy-consuming: processing food crops, providing water and firewood, and caring for the children, elderly and the sick as indicated by the table below

### 3.10 CLIMATE CHANGE AND GENDER

"Climate change is a major threat to the environment and natural resources, which we need for the sustainable development of our globe. Climate change will undermine the very foundation of socioeconomic development and will increase inequality and poverty. It will have a serious impact on the livelihoods of poor women in all income groups, as increasing droughts and storms will affect their access to food and water resources, which are often their responsibility."

Gender is a vital element to be taken into account when considering actions both to mitigate and to adapt to climate change. Climate change impacts are not only economic and physical, but also social. Because of gender differences in the roles, responsibilities, and opportunities, the effects of climate change affect women and men in different ways and often with unequal consequences.

Worldwide climate impacts will be differently distributed among different regions, generations, age, classes, income groups, occupations and genders (IPCC 2011).37 Variability due to climate change is posing specific challenges for Rwanda, including more frequent and intense extreme weather events, such as floods and droughts, which have significant negative impact on natural resources, security, food production and human health.

People's vulnerability and capacity to be resilient and adapt depend in the access to assets. In Rwanda compared to men women tend to have more limited access to resources that would enhance their capacity to adapt to climate change— including land, credit, agricultural inputs, access to markets, decision-making bodies, technology and training services like it has been highlighted previously.

Having less access to asset makes women in Rwanda more vulnerable and less resilient to climate


---
**Page 301**
---

change than men. Women’s coping mechanisms to climate change are still limited due to the high poverty among them, low literacy rate, limited access to extension services and different cultural norms, traditional roles, and power relations between men and women as highlighted above. The GTZ (2010) and the Technical Centre for Agricultural and Rural Cooperation (CTA, 2014) emphasized the vulnerability of women in rural areas to global climate change that, as a rule, poor social groups bear the brunt of climate change—not only because they are more dependent on natural resources, but also because they lack the requisite capacity to adapt to climate change.

If there is no clean drinking water, women must walk longer and more often over rough terrain to look for it. If there is less food, a woman is the last in the family to eat. Thus, climate changes increase the existing gender gaps, and continue to adversely and disproportionately affect women, particularly, smallholder women farmers and pastoralists.

Children and women spend much time on the chores of firewood collection taking them between two hours and three hours. This remains a huge workload for women, limiting their chance to engage in other productive activities. The use of Biomass (Firewood and Charcoal) remains predominant among male and female-headed households as source of cooking energy in the country. Scale up of alternative sources of energy for cooking will reduce workload on women while giving ample time for them to engage in other activities. This will also relieve air pollution and health issues resulting from the use of firewood.21

The National Climate Change Vulnerability Index defines the Eastern Province as the area with the highest levels of vulnerability in the country. Existing gender imbalances between men and women (particularly, traditional gender roles and patriarchal attitudes towards women in rural Rwanda) weaken their adaptive capacity and make them more vulnerable to shocks and stresses linked to climate change. As a result, women bear the most negative effects of climate change-induced disasters.

Primary data findings highlight women’s limited mobility outside their homes, unpaid care work/household chores, and power relations within the households. In fact, in the case of hunger/famine in the households or community, women and children are the most affected, because men can move away from home in search of food or money and can come back home even after one or two months, as indicated by the CTA (2014). The above is confirmed by the results from the EICV 4 as per figure 16.

Therefore, women remain more vulnerable both in droughts and even during the heavy rain seasons and flooding periods.

Climate change has been identified in the EICV4 III as a crosscutting issue that should be mainstreamed across all strategic plans to ensure sustainable and inclusive development, which also is environmentally sustainable. The National Gender Policy Strategic Plan 2016-2020[3] includes among other objectives the government's priorities for environmental protection. It advances this priority by promoting equal participation of men and women in environmental management, through increasing awareness of men and women heads of households on the benefits of radical and progressive terracing for erosion control, and encouraging them to participate in related work. It also stresses increasing the use of biogas for both male- and female-headed households, especially in rural areas.

# Chapter 4: Conclusions

Rwanda has made great efforts to promote economic inclusiveness with special focus on traditionally excluded groups including women. This gender analysis report provides an overview of key policies, legislations and institutional strategies to promote women empowerment and gender equality. It also presented key selected statistics and indicators to highlight progress in economic development and empowerment of women.

The study found that while Rwanda has made impressive strides in the fight against poverty, it is still unable to make up a disproportionate percentage of workers in the informal sector including as domestic workers in subsistence farming systems or seasonal workers. However, while women constitute 66% of the agricultural work force, only 19.7% of women are paid for their labor and lack access-earning opportunities. This is due to gender stereotypes that affect women’s access to appropriate jobs, skills, and responsibilities of men and women whereby men are perceived as breadwinners and providers for their families which restricts women's economic opportunity/autonomy.

The study also focused on understanding the conditions for accessing and controlling productive resources such as access to land (use and ownership rights), agricultural inputs, technology and markets, financial services, education and health; and identified key barriers that hindered women’s access and opportunities for income generation. These include lack of secure tenure/ownership of land (as productive resource itself but also as barrier to access credit), lack of information and training, lack of involvement in decision-making, but also lack of experience and models that demonstrate gender-sensitive approaches. Women are further constrained by limited coping mechanisms or climate change; are further limited due to high poverty, low literacy rates, limited access to extension services and different cultural norms, traditional roles, and power relations between men and women. Women are also more affected by threats to hunger/famine due to prolonged droughts as they provide resources for their children first and because men are more mobile in the search of food or income.

Women are key players in the agricultural sector and their livelihoods are highly dependent on agricultural outputs and access to sustainable energy resources. The project provides important entry points for addressing identified gender gaps and barriers of women farmers and women-headed households and also for improving their ability to benefit from agroforestry and silvopastoral systems.

The findings are summarized in terms of barriers and constraints as well as needs and priorities of women and men should be fully taken into account on board in the detailed design of the project. Therefore the following recommendations are made:

- Ensure that women farmers are provided equal opportunities for training on climate resilient agricultural practices (e.g. agroforestry techniques)
- Identify and promote women entrepreneurs as role models in activities around local enterprise development, e.g. in the context of managing trees nurseries, nursery for fodder trees, value chains etc.


---
**Page 304**
---

- Support women and strengthen female small-holder groups to become a more active and recognized actor in natural resources management (e.g., in the context of woodlots and free plantations, district forests concessions etc.)
- Provide opportunities and build capacity of women leaders, lead farmers, farmer trainers and female-gendered organizations.
- Train women farmers, farmer groups and cooperatives on organizational and financial management to enable access to financing including through mobilization of savings;
- Improve women's access to credit from the supply site (e.g., by improving financial products of microfinance institutions).
- Strengthen women involvement in decision making on site selection and management of water infrastructure provided by the project (water tanks, rainwater harvesting etc.)
- Promote access to sustainable energy sources for household consumption, in particular for women-headed households and poor households
- Ensure women inclusion in central and district level planning and management decisions on agriculture, livestock and forestry

# Gender Action Plan (GAP)

## Integrating a Gender Perspective into Project Activities

The project preparation phase has already provided a first opportunity to study the socio-economic conditions of men and women in Rwanda and in the project area, the relationships between men and women, the different roles, rights, needs and causes of vulnerability as well as opportunities of women and men, boys and girls in the context of this project. The results of this analysis have been documented in the Gender Analysis Report (GAR). This document provides a gender perspective for each of the 10 high-level entry points for the project for promoting gender equality, addressing specific constraints or access and rights issues women face in relation to natural resource management but also opportunities for the project to contribute to reducing gender inequalities. The GAR is based on the assumption that projects using gender-sensitive and effective approaches will be more likely to achieve their objectives while being gender-sensitive and to effectively contribute to reducing gender gaps in terms of climate change-induced social, economic and environmental vulnerabilities.

It is important to understand that the selection of sites and the detailed design of the field interventions (referred to as project activities) will occur during inception phase of the project. Once the actual sites for the field interventions are defined, the project team will drill deeper in the analysis of gender relevant differences and opportunities. This will happen as part of the rapid social baseline analysis planned for each site. The rapid social baseline analysis is a tool that will be applied by the project team with communities and other relevant stakeholders through dedicated and separate consultation of women groups and individuals. Applying such a gender-lens will be critical for designing the field interventions to ensure they are genuinely gender-sensitive, and that the project activities are designed in ways that contribute to the promotion of gender equality so that women and men have equal access to project services and benefits and that unintended negative impacts are avoided. The latter is the focus of the EMS screening of the social baseline analysis which will be conducted as part of the rapid social baseline analysis detailed in the EMS. As explained in the EMS, the rapid social analysis is included in the toolbox that will be applied by the project in the context of the Restoration Opportunity Assessment Methodology (ROAM) (see output 2.1). The ROAM will be used to identify potential restoration opportunities for ESMF sub-projects as well as establishing the social baseline for each site selected for field interventions, including the gender relevant differences and opportunities. The gender specialist (see below) will be involved in the planning of the rapid social analysis and will provide guidance throughout.

## 2. Gender Action Plan

In order to further strengthen gender-sensitivity of project design and provide for gender-responsive approaches/solutions to ensure using gender gaps identified on the gender analysis and to improve gender equality, a Gender Action Plan (GAP) has been developed that guides each output of the high-level and planned activities of the project. It will ensure that innovation and opportunities for livelihood improvement and economic development are guided by principles of gender equality. The GAP which is presented in this document consists of a table of contents followed by a description of measures improving gender under each output. These measures have been developed to provide an additional layer of detail and complements the project activities described in section 6.0 of the Full Proposal by establishing specific

1 The GAP has been updated in March 2021


---
**Page 313**
---

gender elements for those project activities where gender aspects are important. The GAP is a management tool that will be used by the Project Director to implement the Full Action Plan. To monitor progress with the gender measures, each indicator is linked to each, with two targets—one to measure progress at mid-term and a second target to be achieved at project completion. While the majority of the indicators and targets have already been defined, others are to be determined through consultations (indicated in the table with “TBD”). For each of the measures—costs and responsibilities have been defined.

The GAP presented below should be understood as a preliminary Gender Action Plan as it will be revised and fine-tuned once the sites for field interventions have been identified, based on the information resulting from the rapid social assessment. The Gender Action Plan will be used to identify stakeholder groups (men and women) carried out for detailing on-the-ground project interventions. These consultations will be crucial for validating the Project's proposed gender-equity measures, indicators and targets. It is important to note that the Gender Action Plan is a living document and that all of the steps described above (rapid social assessment, consultations and refinement of the Gender Action Plan) will need to be concluded prior to commencing any physical project activity on the ground.

The indicators and targets presented in the Gender Action Plan will implement the gender aspect overarching M&E framework for the project. The indicators are linked to each project activity. The targets established in the GAP need to be understood as additional layer of detail and will ensure that progress of implementing the gender measures can be monitored appropriately.

The PMU is the entity with overall responsibility for ensuring gender-sensitive project implementation and the achievement of the gender targets. The Tasks for the Project Director explicitly require experience with gender-differentiated responses in project execution. In addition, a gender specialist will be recruited by ICSN to carry out the above described women’s stakeholder consultations and further engagement as required. The gender specialist will also provide technical support on the identified indicators and targets. The gender specialist will also provide gender-specific training for the relevant executing agencies’ project teams to ensure these are fully versed in gender-sensitivity and how to reflect this in their project activities. The gender specialist will also be responsible for identifying measures, indictors and targets that need to be adhered to when implementing the respective project activities. The gender specialist will also brief all consultants hired by the project on the GAP and how the measures and targets are linked.

The full list of tasks of the gender specialist features in the last section of the GAP. This section also shows the break-down of the effort and costs foreseen for the different actions. It is important to understand, though, that the GAP presents the effort of the gender specialist in framing the gender-specific measures, indicators and targets. The actual implementation of these will be carried out by the executing agencies during their monitoring. The more fundamental investment in gender mainstreaming is reflected through the actual integration of gender-aspects in project design, hence through the actual project activities. As such, the costs foreseen for the gender specialist are either “cost” or specifies where the gender specialist provides additional technical support to the executing entity.

The Gender Action Plan will be monitored on an annual basis. The general timeline of the implementation of the gender measures within each output is determined by the overall timeframe for project implementation and specific dates are determined through the consultations with women stakeholders.

# Gender Action Plan - as complement of the Project's Results Framework

## Project's Impact Statement
To mainstream gender concerns specifically women issues into climate related policies, strategies, legal and institutional framework to enable women access, participation and contribution for integrated resilience approach that is adaptive and able to support transformation and innovative processes.

### Gender-related aspects:
Women’s coping mechanisms to climate change are still limited due to high poverty, low literacy rates, limited access to resources and services, and gender inequalities. These factors create a significant difference between men and women. In the case of hunger/famine due to prolonged drought, women and children are the first to be affected. Women farmers in particular face additional challenges as they have to bear the burden after one or two months. As women are key players in the agricultural sector this project seeks to address the identified gender-related aspects by mainstreaming gender concerns into climate change adaptation and address the specific needs of women (especially rural women) and enable them to be risk informed and adopt resilient agricultural practices to secure food even in drought periods.

## Project's Outcome Statement
Three major outcomes are being planned:

### Outcome 1: Restored landscapes support climate resilient agro-ecological systems and livelihoods in the Eastern Province

### Outcome 2: Women farmers and communities have resources and capacity to restore, benefit from, and maintain climate-resilient landscapes.

### Outcome 3: Strengthened enabling environment to effectively plan, manage and monitor climate adaptation outcomes from improved land use at national and decentralized levels

### Gender-related aspects:
1. Women farmers are skilled in using climate resilient agricultural practices (e.g. agroforestry techniques, intercropping, diversified techniques).
2. Women farmers, groups and cooperatives are skilled and knowledgeable on organizational management and finance and apply techniques to increase resilience of selected value chains and to provide food security.
3. Local and National Institutions and governance promote gender mainstreaming as mechanisms to enhance capacities to implement adaptation strategies and manage climate change

1. Introduction

### 1.1. Purpose of the Access Restriction Mitigation Process Framework

This Access Restriction Mitigation Process (Framework) (PF) was prepared to provide a governing framework and technical guidance for the process of preparation and implementation of Action Plans to mitigate impacts from Access Restrictions (ARs) on land users, particularly in Rwanda. The PF is based on the Transboundary Regional Environmental Project Approach through Adaptation (TREPA) Project (the Project) in Rwanda. The PF and AR Action Plans aim to ensure adequate, fair and timely mitigation of the impacts of access restrictions (ARs) on the livelihoods of economically active land users, particularly smallholder farmers, pastoralists, and other vulnerable entities which may necessitate AR with moderate livelihood impacts, in order to help restore degraded landscapes.

The Project will select subjects in various geographical locations and design their specific project interventions. The PF is intended for use by all subjects involved in the Project. At this stage it is not known under which subjects and project activities access restrictions may be imposed. An Action Plan for each subject will be prepared, with a focus on ARs to be considered after the selection of subprojects and screening for potential AR impacts have been accomplished.

3. Accordingly, the preparation of a Process Framework to guide the preparation of AR Action Plans is required by the Project Implementation Strategy (PIS), the General Environmental Strategy (GES), the Environmental and Social Management System of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the Access Restriction Mitigation Policy (ARMP) and the Rwanda Forest Authority (RFA).

4. The PF analyzes applicable legal and policy framework and defines a Project Action Restriction Policy with eligibility criteria and entitlements for displaced project affected persons (PAPs). It sets out procedural requirements, including but not limited to: identification of ARs; public participation (including screening, social impact assessment, stakeholder engagement (consultation, participation, disclosure and grievance redress), provision of mitigation measures, monitoring and reporting, as well as the institutional and financial arrangements for implementation.

5. This PF was prepared by IUCN and is endorsed by the Ministry of Environment (MoE) through the Rwanda Forest Authority (RFA). The Executive Unit (EU) of the project, RFA, ENABEL and IUCN Rwanda, will be responsible for its implementation in the Project.

6. The PF complies with the applicable laws of Rwanda, as well as the Environmental and Social Policy of GEF and the Environmental and Social Management System of IUCN, in accordance with the CITES ESM Principles and Criteria. It is intended to ensure that all ARs are justified by a clear rationale and, where the safeguard requirements providing stronger protection to project affected persons will prevail.

7. The PF is an integral component of the Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) for the TREPA Project. It complements the ESMF and the Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP).

# Legal and Regulatory Framework for Access Restrictions

## Rwanda Legal and Regulatory Framework

### 23. With the ratification of the 1994 Constitution of Rwanda and the Organic Law No R/025/01 of 16/11/2011 Governing Land in Rwanda (amending Organic Law No 08/2002 of 14/7/2003), the country is transitioning its land tenure system from traditional customary laws to a system of land ownership by the state and private legal persons.

- **Traditional customary laws:** Although varying between regions and local social groups, were generally based on tribal lineage codes allocating land to their descendants, or on kings and war chiefs maintaining control over large areas. These laws also regulated access to grazing and agricultural land.
  - In principle, customary law recognized land use rights through three modes of acquisition: inheritance, gift, and purchase. It allowed for the division of land into smaller plots, enabling new land to which no chief held full claim; thus, recognizing both collective and individual ownership.

- **Colonial era and post-independence period:** Codified private property or possession rights of land occupied by individuals, with a system of registration and title deeds. This led to conflicts between customary laws and the state's legal framework.
  - The current Land Act provides for freehold ownership of land as well as long-term leasehold of state land by individuals and entities.

- **State ownership:** Of land is divided into two categories: (i) state land in the public domain, including lakes and rivers and their shores, natural forests, national parks, protected swamps and national roads; and their boundaries are defined by law. (ii) State-owned land acquired through purchase, donation or expropriation for a public purpose, as well as unprotected swamps and state-owned forests.
  - For protected areas and national parks, the 2004 National Parks Act provides for the establishment of buffer zones around these areas to ensure the involvement of neighboring communities in the conservation of protected areas through creation and strengthening of local institutions. The Act also provides for the establishment of the Akagera National Park and its boundaries, as well as a buffer zone and an economic development zone.

- **No specific provisions:** In the respective land and forest laws that grant local community members general use rights over land owned by the state and its resources, such as degraded District and State-owned forests. These areas are also subject to conservation measures, including afforestation and river shoreline and roadside plantations and the buffer zone of the Akagera National Park, which are targeted for restoration of their landscapes under the Project. Activities not explicitly permitted and

regulated by state authorities are considered illegal and prohibited, as under Article 26 of the 2013 Law Determining the Management and Utilization of Forests in Rwanda. Regulated use of the forest is confined may be granted to local authorities for purposes of agriculture, livestock rearing, or other economic basis. For example, the 2013 Forest Law allows for the reservation of land for crops and livestock and planting of agricultural trees on private lands. The law also provides for the establishment of a national forest fund and its regulated use, and Articles 40 and 42 permit the transfer of management rights for State or District Forests to local authorities or other entities under certain conditions.

Under Chapter VII licensing of specified forest use activities, including for the collection and sale of forest products, is permitted. However, under Article 23 harvesting of forests and collection of forest products may be suspended in areas where they are considered illegal.

28. Thus, collection of fallen branches and dead wood for firewood, collection of fruits and other food plants, or the harvesting of specified amounts of timber for construction of local homes and other buildings, as well as the cutting of trees for fuelwood, is permitted on authorized land only upon authorization by official of the respective authorities, often on the initiative of local leaders.

29. However, provisions stipulating the payment of compensation for the illegal use of access rights are not standard in Rwanda. The law does not provide for compensation to be paid to unauthorized land users.

30. The Law No 5/2015 of 7/1/2015 Relating to Expropriation in the Public Interest governs involuntary land acquisition and resettlement but makes no provisions for involuntary restriction of access to resources and land use. Involuntary expropriation is not applied under the Project, which does not entail involuntary land acquisition and resettlement.

3.2. IUCN and GCF Standards

1. Safeguards are provided for the management of restrictions on access to resources and land use are provided in the Environmental and Social Policy of the Green Climate Fund and the Environmental and Social Management System of IUCN. GCF has adopted the performance standards of the International Finance Corporation (IFC) Performance Standard 5 (PS 5), which includes provisions for involuntary expropriation and Involuntary Resettlement (IP 5). IUCN has formulated the Standard on Involuntary Resettlement and Access Restrictions (IAR).

32. This section focuses primarily on the safeguard requirements for access restriction both GCF and IUCN, as the Project does not entail involuntary land acquisition and resettlement. The requirements of the respective standards are presented separately in this document and will be presented concurrently. Relevant differences will be pointed out as appropriate.

Both standards cover physical displacement (relocation or loss of shelter) and economic displacement (loss of livelihoods due to restrictions on access to resources, sometimes other means of livelihood), as a result of project-related land acquisition and/or restrictions on land use.

3. They apply the mitigation hierarchy requiring projects to avoid and minimize displacement to the maximum extent possible. Where avoidance is not feasible or practical, then minimization measures are mandated. Unavoidable AI impacts are to be minimized and mitigated by providing compensation of lost assets and services, including housing, education, health care, and other social services for displaced persons. In case of physical displacement, the provision of adequate housing with security of tenure is required. Where economic displacement occurs, there should be disclosure of information, consultation, and the informed participation of those affected. IUCN requires that a Community Participation Committee (CPC) of persons or communities affected by restriction of access.

35. IUCN PS 5 applies to all projects where project situations where involuntary restrictions on land use and access to natural resources cause a community or groups within a community to lose access to resource usage where they have traditional or recognizable usage rights, as well as AI restriction on access to land and resources for the purposes of agriculture, livestock rearing, fishing, hunting, gathering, and aquatic resources, timber and non-timber forest products, freshwater, medicinal plants, hunting and gathering areas, and other natural resources.

36. While IUCN PS 5 indicates its applicability to AI for communities with traditional or recognizable usage rights as well as for communal property, it also refers to a range of natural resources without specifying the


---
**Page 333**
---

property status of their resource users. It moreover notes that affected persons frequently do not have formal ownership rights. Furthermore, PS is classified persons who have no recognizable legal right or claim to the land and resources they use or occupy. PAPs are defined as persons with a recognized legal right or claim to mitigation of impacts, in addition to persons with formal legal rights or legally recognizable claims to land or assets.

37. IUCN's standard indicates as within the scope of its application (i) the restriction of access and/or use of natural resources and to areas of occupation or use, as well as (ii) changes in the use and management regime of such resources and areas. The standard applies to all types of land tenure systems, including land and resource users. It states nevertheless that all losses must be considered as legitimate for compensation, including those resulting from customary and/or legal tenure and resource use regimes, but excludes those that involve illegal activity.

38. The general requirements of the standards applicable to AI include the following:

• Establishment of the applicability of the performance standard through the environmental and social data collection process, including baseline information on displaced persons and their livelihoods.
• Involvement of affected communities through stakeholder engagement, including information disclosure, consultation, participation and a grievance mechanism, during the assessment, planning, implementation and monitoring phases.

• Census and social impact assessment to provide baseline information, assess AR impacts on displaced persons and to determine their eligibility for mitigation measures.
• Special attention to the needs of and issues affecting poor and vulnerable people and groups, including women and children.
• Preparation of action plans for the mitigation of AI impacts, which indicate the eligibility and entitlements of PAPs to mitigation measures, identify development opportunities, and develop a resettlement plan where appropriate.

• Responsibility of the project for the cost of implementation of action plans.
• Preparation of process frameworks for the mitigation of AR impacts, which guide the preparation and implementation of action plans. This is particularly important where the exact nature and magnitude of impacts are not known during the project development stage.
• Compensation of losses at replacement cost (value) i.e., the amount necessary to replace the lost assets or resources, including compensation in kind for goods and services generated by the lost assets.
• Land based compensation for displaced persons with land-based livelihoods.
• Provision of mitigation measures before displacement.
• Provision of appropriate project benefits.
• Establishment of procedures for monitoring and evaluation of the implementation of mitigation plans.
• Disclosure and approval of action plans and frameworks for the mitigation of AR impacts by GCF and IUCN.

39. In the case of economic displacement action plans establish the eligibility and entitlements displaced persons to ensure the restoration and improvement of their livelihoods, including

• Compensation at replacement cost or value of lost land and other assets of persons with formal legal rights or claims to land.
• Compensation at replacement cost or value of lost assets other than land of persons without formal legal rights or claims to land, and


---
**Page 334**
---

40. For persons affected by project-related restriction of access mitigation measures are provided to either allow continued access to affected resources or access to alternative resources with equivalent livelihood earning potential. These include provision of land for agricultural purposes, where feasible, culturally appropriate alternative income earning opportunities may be provided, such as credit facilities and microfinance, and employment opportunities facilitating livelihood restoration with equivalent livelihood earning potential.

41. In the case of physical displacement action plans establish the eligibility and entitlements of displaced persons to adequate housing, land tenure security, compensation for loss of assets, and provision of security of tenure or cash compensation at full replacement cost, as well as adequate relocation assistance, including access to education and health services. Displaced persons will be provided with land titles so that displaced persons without titles or claims to land need to be provided with adequate housing with security of tenure so that they can legally settle without having to face the risk of forced eviction.

42. To provide for resettlement of displaced persons in the project area a relevant government authority establishes and manages public and private land for eligible displaced persons.

### 3. Gap Analysis

The preceding analysis indicates the absence of a general legal and policy framework in Rwanda for the restriction of access to resources and land use, and for the assessment and mitigation of related adverse social impacts. By contrast GEF/IFC and IUCN have established safeguard standards to protect the livelihoods of displaced persons and communities affected by projects that impact on forests, wetlands, rivers, lakes, and the management of protected landscapes and resources. Although community participation in the management of resources in protected areas or other state lands is permitted under Rwandan law, there is no comprehensive legal framework for the assessment and mitigation of social impacts related to displaced resource users. Accordingly, in the TREFPA Project the impact of all AR will be carried out in accordance with the international standards set by IFC/GEF.

44. The above analysis also points out the weaknesses of traditional customary land rights systems and land use practices under Rwanda's contemporary legal and regulatory system. However, poor and vulnerable rural communities are often unable to access formal land tenure security or compensation for loss of assets but frequently unlimited accessibility of open resources owned by the state, given their limited levels of livelihood earning potential. The project area is located in a zone where customary land rights systems are not recognized under Rwandan law. In addition, the project area falls within the boundaries of areas managed by the project (District and State-owned tree plantations, lake and river shoreline and roadside plantations and the buffer zone of the Aleraga National Park) often represent critical natural resource assets for resource users in terms of livelihood earning potential, but are not recognized under Rwandan law as basis for subsistence and for gaining income by small-scale commercialization.

45. The Project will therefore pay particular attention to the needs of vulnerable groups displaced by AR, especially women, elderly persons, disabled persons, orphans and children, ethnic minorities, or other displaced persons whose land use practices may not be protected under national legislation. PAPs experience that these groups are often unable to access formal land tenure security or compensation for AR related impacts, in accordance with the IFC/GEF provision recognizing persons without formal legal rights or claims to land as vulnerable and requiring project proponents to provide adequate housing and other assistance.

46. The project does not include activities that require involuntary land acquisition or resettlement. The project also expressly excludes any physical displacement due to access restriction, including of non-titled sections of the project area, from its definition of involuntary land acquisition or resettlement.

47. According to, to safeguard persons affected by AR and especially vulnerable communities, and to mitigate the impacts of AR on them, the project will implement the following access restriction policy.

# Project Access Restriction Policy

## Screening
- Each prospective subproject under the project will be screened to assess whether Access Restrictions will be required to manage its landscape restoration activities and thereby trigger the requirements for the preparation and implementation of an Action Plan to Mitigate Impacts from Access Restrictions.

## AR Planning
- Each subproject which proposes AR will prepare a comprehensive Action Plan to Mitigate Impacts from Access Restrictions.
- Each Draft and Final AR Action Plan will be submitted to IUCN for review and approval, endorsed by the RFA, and disclosed on the IUCN and RFA websites.
- In the case of anticipated AR impacts noted after AR Action Plan finalization and approval, updated AR Action Plans will be prepared in accordance with the above process.

## Stakeholder Engagement
- All AR will be led by the stakeholder engagement activities relevant to AR will be included in the Stakeholder Engagement Plan.
- Displaced persons and other stakeholders will be consulted and informed about the planned access restrictions and their impact on them, and given an opportunity to participate in the planning of AR in an accessible, understandable and culturally appropriate form. AR mitigation measures will be negotiated with the IPs and their free, prior and informed consent will be obtained before the implementation of any AR.
- Draft AR Action Plans, including drafts of updated AR Action Plans, will be disclosed to PAFs for review and comments. The approved final AR Action Plans will be disclosed to the PAFs as well. All stakeholders will have an opportunity to provide feedback on the staff's draft and updated AR Action Plans.

## A grievance redress mechanism with representation of relevant stakeholders will be established at the time of project inception, which will be accessible to persons displaced by AR and will endeavor to resolve their grievances promptly and transparently.


### Vulnerable Project Affected Persons
- Vulnerability assessments for the specific AR impacts on their livelihoods will be identified in the census and socio-economic survey for each subproject and indicated in each Action Plan. The inclusion of displaced vulnerable persons in consultations and the planning of measures for the rehabilitation and empowerment of displaced vulnerable persons will be undertaken to reduce poverty, impoverishment and to reduce their vulnerability.

# Assessment of AR Impacts

- A comprehensive social impact assessment (SIA) of all persons displaced by AR, an inventory of their lost resources and assets, a limited socio-economic baseline survey, and an assessment of the economic value of lost assets and incomes will be carried out.
- On the basis of the assessment of actual AR impacts under a subproject, the SIA will be used to determine eligibility conditions for eligibility and entitlements under the Project AR Policy will be triggered and are applicable.

## Eligibility

- Persons displaced by access restrictions imposed and/or enforced under the project, including those with and without formally recognized land use or ownership rights, who use or occupy restricted land and its resources before the cut-off date, will be eligible for mitigation of adverse impacts.
- The eligibility conditions will apply irrespective of whether the impacts are permanent or temporary, full or partial. Not all PAPs without legally recognizable claims to land will be eligible for compensation.
- An eligibility cut-off date will be declared and widely publicized on the date of commencement of the social impact assessment for each subproject which requires AR, to ensure the exclusion of opportunistic encroachment from eligibility for mitigation measures.

## Entitlements

- Compensation of the loss of livelihoods due to the loss of access to resources assets will be done at replacement value, either through mutually agreed continued and regulated access to affected resources or through cash compensation. The choice between these two options is based on accessibility.
- In cases where access to the same or alternative resources are not feasible, culturally appropriate mitigation measures such as provision of land for cultivation, agricultural training opportunities, training, credit facilities, or cash compensation to facilitate livelihood restoration with equivalent livelihood earning potential will be provided.
- In case of loss of livestock and/or poultry due to AR, these will be replaced with assets of equivalent or higher value and quality or through cash compensation at replacement cost, calculated at fair market value plus transaction costs, including interest accrued, transitional and restoration costs and other relevant costs. The value of the lost animals will be determined by a qualified appraiser.
- Transaction costs will be paid by the project or included in compensation payments to the PAPs. The value of the livestock and/or poultry lost due to AR will be considered as the maximum amount for claims to land will be eligible for all mitigation measures, except for the compensation of the loss of land.
- Relocated displaced people, if any, will receive secure tenure to replacement land, better housing, transitional support and access to available civic infrastructure and services.
- For all persons displaced by AR full access to the development benefits under the Project will be ensured. This includes access to resources for sustainable use and conservation of sustainable resource use and conservation under each subproject constitute a key mitigation measure for the impacts on biodiversity and other natural resources in the community resource management activities as well as measures for individual project beneficiaries.
- All agreed mitigation measures must be provided and/or in place12 before access restrictions become effective.

## 5.2 - Capacity Building

The staff of the Executing Entities and of the Service Providers involved in the implementation of subprojects throughout the Project will participate in training workshops on social safeguards for the restriction of access to resource and land use. The training will consist of two modules.

The first module is a classroom-based training, which will be carried out by designated project staff with general overview of the policy and legal requirements for AR under the Project and the preparation of the Process Frameworks.

The second module consists of field-based training, which will be carried out in the context of the first subproject described above. The training will be based on a combination of classroom instruction and practical job instruction and experience. Instruments for the assessment of AR impacts, including formats for the questionnaires to be used by project staff during the field visits, as well as the procedures of FAOs and land asset, will be developed and refined in the context of the training.

The training concept may require the use of an alternative mode of instruction if conditions due to the global COVID-19 health emergency prevent face-to-face training and international travel.

# Stakeholder Engagement

## 60. Meaningful stakeholder engagement (SE) is a critical tool to facilitate the successful implementation of the Project and will be an important element that plays a central role in the management of social impacts caused by the restriction of access to resources and land use.

### 61. SE under each subproject will be commensurate with the level and magnitude of AE impacts. It is involved:

- Screening of subprojects for AR impacts,
- Assessment of all AR impacts and identification of PAPs,
- Establishment and implementation of appropriate mitigation measures, and
- Monitoring and evaluation of the implementation of the subproject AR Action Plans.

### 62. SE for the management of access restrictions involves

- Consultation of all PAPs under a subproject,
- Disclosure of information on the nature of access restriction to mitigate it, including draft and final AR Action Plans for subprojects imposing AR as indicated in the Project Action Under SE in Section 4.
- Participation of PAPs in the negotiation of and decisions on all mitigation measures, as well as the provision of mitigation measures, and
- Establishment of a grievance mechanism.

### 63. In compliance with the requirement for FPIC, the implementation of all project measures with access restrictions and their mitigation will be negotiated with the PAPs and their consent will be obtained in order to go ahead with the project.

### 64. The key methodologies for SE are consistent with standard participatory appraisal practices (see section 7).

#### Focus group discussions and key informant interviews with various sub-sections of the persons displayed by AR (according to gender, socio-economic status, vulnerability types of livelihood activities, etc.) and other relevant project stakeholders for in-depth discussions and the negotiation of AR Action Plans.

#### Plenary meetings with all persons displayed by AR, segregated by gender and other social variables if relevant, and other relevant project stakeholders to: i) provide relevant information and disclose the results of the focus group discussion; ii) discuss the draft AR Action Plan and seek feedback from PAPs receive feedback and address PAP concerns during planning and implementation of AR; and iii) discuss the final AR Action Plan.

#### Participatory resource mapping to identify resource use practices and their locations, and field visits with transect walks in the landscapes and ecosystems under restrictions to observe and discuss in-depth the PAP's resource use practices, their locations, and adverse impacts of AR.

### 65. All SE communication will be undertaken in an accessible, understandable and culturally appropriate form.

### 7.1 Participatory appraisal

As stated above, the sensitive nature of non-titled resource use by mainly poor and vulnerable households in the SIA area requires simultaneous rapport building and an in-depth assessment of AR impacts through participatory appraisal methods, to gain familiarity with the context and develop trust. Therefore, it is recommended that project staff members who are involved in the SIA process ensure that they are aware of the importance of confidentiality and anonymity for public disclosure will only use information gathered from the PAPs. The choice of participatory appraisal methods for this assessment is consistent with and overlaps with the stakeholder engagement approach indicated in section 6.

The purpose of such impacts will focus on establishing the level and magnitude of impacts taking into account the following factors:

- **Nature or type of impact:** What natural resource assets are affected and how?
- **Purpose of resource use:** Are the resources used for subsistence or commercial use?
- **Persons affected:** Who is affected? Are men and women, poor and vulnerable or well-off persons, or major landholders affected by AR impacts?
- **Duration of the impact:** Are access restriction short-term, medium-term, long-term, or permanent?
- **Severity of the impact:** Do the resources losses constitute a large or small proportion of the livelihood assets that are owned or used by the affected person, household and community (taking into account the duration of impacts).

The participatory appraisal will combine several assessment methods. It is critical to allow for sufficient time to ensure that all PAPs have an opportunity to participate in the process. The project staff must be aware of timing and pacing of activities with having to take into account people's obligations and schedules to pursue their livelihood activities and other commitments. Establishment of rapport and trust and gaining access to knowledge and information is a key element for participatory appraisal methods, which require that exercise is very much about listening and learning from the PAPs about their lives, activities, problems and concerns. The project staff must be open-minded in order to understand the PAPs' perspectives on life and think. During the SIA, the project staff needs to suspend preconceived notions and assumptions and be open to new insights and understanding before suggesting and negotiating how to resolve problems and mitigate impacts.

The following approaches and methods to participatory appraisal can be used:

- **Key informant interviews:** are used to discuss a topic in-depth with identified key persons who have extensive knowledge of the area. Key informants may include local government officials, representatives of authorities, trust and influence. Examples include religious leaders, chiefs, successful farmers, and traditional leaders.
- **Response groups:** are used for group discussions on specific topics or issues that are relevant to PAPs in their communities or even regions and may be able to help generate support by and the cooperation of the PAPs.


---
**Page 342**
---

86. Focus group discussions (FGDs) provide opportunities for detailed discussion with a small group of selected participants. Groups can be formed with the participation of a heterogeneous group or by forming a homogeneous group. The facilitator should ensure that the group size is manageable and allow certain groups to speak up (e.g., the poor and vulnerable PAPs, women or marginalized groups) or to focus on specific issues. It may also be useful for the facilitator to ask questions about the following: whether sensitive issues around resource use, the legality of access, livelihoods, well-being, health or issues of marginalization are raised during the discussion; if so, how they were addressed and what was done with the questionnaire, so that the facilitator of the discussion can keep the discussion on track and the participants can expand on topics and raise their own. Documenting the questions asked will also allow the team to reflect on the issues raised by the participants and to identify areas for further research. Mapping around unconscious limited use of resources, formal recording of discussions may be needed to avoid it.

87. Participatory mapping exercises can be used to identify AIR impacts and to develop All Action Plans. The exercise should involve a group discussion with PAPs who are representative of the communities or poverty and vulnerability combined with wealth ranking. Through these exercises the location of resources, their use, and the potential adverse impacts of AIR on them need to be identified using colored markers on large paper or with various different colored materials, such as sand and wood, on the floor of the meeting room. The exercise should also identify the most important resource concern, such as resource use, the composition of ecosystems and livelihood system, the AIR impacts on these systems, differential impacts on the poor and vulnerable or alternative arrangements for resource use. Mapping exercises can be repeated over time to assess changes in resource use patterns and/or changes in terms of respective livelihood activities.

88. Field visits with transect walks in the landscapes and ecosystems under planned restrictions help the project team understand the current land use practices, their locations, and the potential adverse impacts of AIR, and to gain an in-depth understanding in situ. It is important to undertake these walks with the various stakeholders involved in the project (e.g., PAPs, local government officials) so that all issues are covered. Seasonal changes may need to be considered and walks repeated over time. At minimum it needs to cover the dry season and the wet season, but also other seasons if possible, such as the rainy season and how they have changed over time, in particular considering the potential impacts of climate change. Replication of specific walks will be needed to use assess possible mitigation measures in the same or alternative landscapes. The focus should be on identifying critical issues and sites that should be undertaken during the walks, keeping in mind the possible concerns of resource users.

89. The findings of the participatory appraisal with affected local stakeholders and community members will be documented in the All Action Plans for the subprojects for each site visited and discussed, including

* **The number and types of PAPs,** 
* **Locations visited and observed,** 
* **Records of mapped resources,** 
* **Inventories of affected resources and assets and their uses and by affected persons,** 
* **Records of issues discussed and proposed solutions including possible mitigation measures,** and
* **Evidence of participation, including signed minutes or records of participation or photographs or videos, with the appropriate level about anonymity if required or requested.**

90. The project team will use the findings for the participatory appraisal as a basis for interpretation and analysis of the findings of the participatory appraisal for each site under the subproject planned to go under restrictions. The narrative analysis can be supported and illustrated by a descriptive table for the main variables assessed, including

* **the use of the resource,**

93. The types of resources users potentially affected by AR in the subproject areas would likely be predominantly PAs without formally recognized land use or ownership rights. A smaller group of MA may be expected to be impacted as they have formal recognition of their land tenure, either through customary law or a legal instrument recognized or recognizable under the national laws, such as persons with tenures for resources issued by government agencies. The impact on these groups would affect person or legal entities owning private land or land leased from the government.
94. Among the potential PAHs the following groups may be expected:
- Returning refugees or people affected by competing claims from resettlers: Rwanda has seen the return of many refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the past. For example, two-thirds of the land area of the Abatana National Park was allotted to refugees and demobilized soldiers after the 1994 genocide. The same land area is now being offered for resettlement by settlers under the Land Tenure Regularization Program resulting in competing claims for land and temporary or long-term land tenures.
- Pastoralists: This group includes even and land occupied by pastoralists. Restriction of access to grazing land might affect transhumant communities, competition for water and pastures due to the increased length of droughts may increase pressure on range lands. People who have been displaced from their traditional land or whose reserved land parcels might be too small to sustain a household and provide for sufficient resources.
95. Landless people: The Land Tenure Regularization Program provided an opportunity to all Rwandan citizens to claim land, but the process was not inclusive of all groups in society. As such, through an inclusive process, there may be vulnerable groups who were not able to file their land claims during the formal regularization process. These may therefore be landless and highly dependent on open land and forest resources for their livelihoods.
92. Censuses of persons affected by access restrictions
96. The participatory appraisal methods permit an in-depth understanding of resource use in locations under government control, including areas with access restrictions or limitations. However, by using participatory appraisal methods the data generated is based on the observation of the various individuals and groups available for meetings, discussions and walks and can therefore not provide a complete inventory of all persons affected by AR. The census will be conducted through a household survey, through a full census including a limited socio-economic survey (SES) of all PAHs affected by AR. The census enumeration will be carried out in the field using trained enumerators, deployed households, using a closed-ended questionnaire querying all relevant variables, including:
- Number of displaced households and all their members,
- Types and quantities of all resource assets affected by AR, and their associated property status,
- All monetary income (e.g., agricultural production, livestock, fishing, business, employment etc.) and total monetary and non-monetary income among all household members, and
- All other property of land, buildings and other structures not affected by AR and their associated property status.
